subtopic_detail: Coeliac disease testing after self-initiated gluten avoidance
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 34 year old woman referred with eight months of bloating and loose stools. She has iron deficiency anaemia that has not corrected despite six months of documented adherence to oral ferrous sulfate, and her gastroscopy request has not yet been triaged.

After reading about her symptoms online she removed all gluten from her diet seven weeks ago and reports her bowels have settled. She has no red flag features, no family history of bowel cancer and menstruates normally with a cycle she describes as light. Coeliac serology has not previously been performed.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg/m2, abdomen soft and non-tender, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155); ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-200); C-reactive protein and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Request HLA DQ2 and DQ8 typing and manage according to the result
options.rationale: HLA typing is a rule-out test with high negative predictive value but poor positive predictive value, since roughly half the Australian population carries a permissive haplotype, so a positive result cannot establish the diagnosis (Source: GESA Clinical Update: Coeliac Disease).

options.text: Request tissue transglutaminase IgA and total IgA on the current diet
options.rationale: Serology falls with gluten withdrawal and after seven weeks off gluten a negative result cannot be interpreted, which is the near-pair trap against testing after a challenge (Source: GESA Clinical Update: Coeliac Disease).

options.text: Reintroduce gluten for at least six weeks, then test transglutaminase and total IgA
options.rationale: Both serology and duodenal histology require active gluten exposure, so a documented challenge of about four slices of bread daily for six weeks restores diagnostic accuracy before testing (Source: GESA Clinical Update: Coeliac Disease; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

options.text: Proceed directly to gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies while she avoids gluten
options.rationale: Villous architecture recovers on a gluten free diet, so biopsy taken now risks a false negative and commits her to endoscopy that may need repeating (Source: GESA Clinical Update: Coeliac Disease).

options.text: Continue gluten avoidance and give intravenous ferric carboxymaltose now
options.rationale: Correcting the iron without a diagnosis leaves a lifelong condition unlabelled, forfeits family screening and removes the only window in which testing is accurate (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Coeliac disease is diagnosed on serology plus duodenal histology, and both depend on ongoing gluten exposure. Patients who start a gluten free diet before testing create a diagnostic dead end that can only be resolved by a formal gluten challenge or by HLA typing to exclude the diagnosis. A confirmed diagnosis matters beyond symptom control because it triggers first degree relative screening, bone density assessment and long term dietitian involvement that an unconfirmed self-diagnosis does not. Iron deficiency anaemia refractory to oral replacement is one of the commonest presentations in adults, often with minimal bowel symptoms.
key_points: Serology and histology are only valid on a gluten containing diet
Gluten challenge is about four slices of bread daily for at least six weeks before testing
Total IgA is measured alongside transglutaminase IgA because selective IgA deficiency causes false negatives
HLA DQ2 and DQ8 typing excludes rather than confirms coeliac disease
Confirmed diagnosis triggers first degree relative screening and bone density assessment
explanation.pearls: Selective IgA deficiency is about ten times more common in coeliac disease than in the general population, which is why total IgA is always ordered with the transglutaminase IgA rather than after a negative result.

subtopic_detail: Helicobacter pylori eradication with penicillin hypersensitivity
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 47 year old man in the gastroenterology clinic after a gastroscopy performed for three months of epigastric pain. The endoscopist found a 1 cm clean based duodenal ulcer and rapid urease testing on antral biopsies was positive.

At age nineteen he developed a widespread urticarial rash with lip swelling within an hour of an amoxicillin dose and has avoided all penicillins since. He has never taken a macrolide and has not travelled outside Australia. He takes no regular medicines and stopped ibuprofen four weeks ago when the pain began.

data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness, no guarding, no mass
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-175); renal and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: Which eradication regimen is most appropriate to prescribe?

options.text: Esomeprazole with clarithromycin and metronidazole twice daily for seven days
options.rationale: This is the standard Australian first line substitution when amoxicillin cannot be used, and it retains two active antibiotics with a proton pump inhibitor for the full seven day course (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Esomeprazole with amoxicillin and clarithromycin twice daily for seven days
options.rationale: A history of urticaria with angioedema within an hour of a dose is immediate hypersensitivity, so amoxicillin is contraindicated without formal allergy assessment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

options.text: Esomeprazole twice daily alone for eight weeks and repeat the gastroscopy
options.rationale: Acid suppression heals the ulcer but leaves the organism in place, and untreated infection carries a high one year recurrence rate compared with successful eradication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

options.text: Esomeprazole with levofloxacin and amoxicillin twice daily for ten days
options.rationale: Quinolone based regimens are reserved for second or third line salvage after treatment failure, and this one still contains the implicated penicillin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

options.text: Esomeprazole with clarithromycin and metronidazole twice daily for three days
options.rationale: Shortening the course below seven days materially reduces eradication rates and is the commonest avoidable cause of persistent infection (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Australian first line eradication is a proton pump inhibitor with amoxicillin and clarithromycin for seven days, with metronidazole substituting for amoxicillin in genuine penicillin hypersensitivity. Eradication is confirmed at least four weeks after finishing antibiotics and at least one week after stopping the proton pump inhibitor, usually by urea breath test. Duodenal ulcers associated with the organism do not require maintenance acid suppression once eradication is confirmed, unlike ulcers driven by ongoing anti-inflammatory use. Clarithromycin resistance is the dominant reason for failure and rises sharply with prior macrolide exposure, which is why the prescribing history matters.
key_points: First line is a proton pump inhibitor with amoxicillin and clarithromycin for seven days
Metronidazole replaces amoxicillin in immediate penicillin hypersensitivity
Confirm eradication four weeks after antibiotics and one week off the proton pump inhibitor
Prior macrolide exposure predicts clarithromycin resistance and guides regimen choice
Quinolone containing regimens are salvage therapy, not first line
explanation.pearls: A urea breath test performed while the patient is still taking a proton pump inhibitor gives false negatives, so the drug is withheld for at least seven days before the confirmatory test.

subtopic_detail: Acute severe colitis initial inpatient management
stem:
You are the admitting medical registrar for a 23 year old woman with a two year history of ulcerative colitis maintained on mesalazine. Over eight days she has had up to nine bloody stools daily including two overnight, with cramping that wakes her.

She has taken no anti-inflammatory drugs and has not travelled or taken antibiotics recently. Stool testing for Clostridioides difficile and for enteric pathogens is negative and cytomegalovirus serology is pending. Abdominal radiograph shows no colonic dilatation and no free gas.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 108/66, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with generalised tenderness, bowel sounds present, no rebound
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-155); white cells 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5); albumin 28 g/L (35-50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 40 mg daily with an increase in the mesalazine dose
options.rationale: Oral steroids are for ambulatory moderate disease, and absorption is unreliable once a patient meets severe criteria with hypoalbuminaemia (Source: GESA Inflammatory Bowel Disease Guidelines).

options.text: Intravenous infliximab as a single induction dose with oral mesalazine continued
options.rationale: Biologic rescue is the decision made at day three when the steroid response is judged inadequate, not the opening move before steroids have been given (Source: GESA Inflammatory Bowel Disease Guidelines).

options.text: Intravenous ciprofloxacin and metronidazole with intravenous fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not treat the underlying inflammation and are reserved for suspected perforation or toxic megacolon, neither of which is present on the radiograph (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

options.text: Urgent surgical referral for consideration of subtotal colectomy within 24 hours
options.rationale: Surgery lives on a different decision axis and is reserved for perforation, haemorrhage, toxic dilatation or failed medical rescue, none of which applies on day one (Source: GESA Inflammatory Bowel Disease Guidelines).

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone with prophylactic enoxaparin and fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Intravenous corticosteroid is first line for acute severe colitis, and thromboprophylaxis is given despite rectal bleeding because active colitis is a strong prothrombotic state (Source: GESA Inflammatory Bowel Disease Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

explanation.summary: Acute severe colitis is defined by six or more bloody stools daily plus a marker of systemic upset such as tachycardia, fever, anaemia or a raised inflammatory response. Admission management is intravenous corticosteroid, fluid and electrolyte correction, exclusion of superimposed infection and pharmacological thromboprophylaxis. Response is formally assessed on day three using stool frequency and C-reactive protein, and inadequate response triggers rescue therapy with infliximab or ciprofloxacin sparing alternatives alongside early surgical involvement. Delay at that decision point is the main driver of emergency colectomy and its complications.
key_points: Six or more bloody stools daily plus systemic upset defines acute severe colitis
Intravenous corticosteroid is first line, not oral prednisolone
Thromboprophylaxis is given despite rectal bleeding
Exclude Clostridioides difficile and cytomegalovirus before escalating immunosuppression
Day three response assessment decides rescue therapy versus continued steroid
explanation.pearls: On day three of intravenous steroid, more than eight stools daily, or three to eight stools with a C-reactive protein above 45 mg/L, predicts about an 85 per cent chance of colectomy and mandates rescue therapy that day.

subtopic_detail: Ascitic fluid analysis and infection management in cirrhosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 58 year old man with alcohol related cirrhosis and a two day history of increasing abdominal distension and diffuse discomfort. He stopped drinking eleven months ago and takes spironolactone and frusemide.

He is alert and orientated with no asterixis. A diagnostic paracentesis is performed on arrival before any antibiotic is given. Blood cultures are collected at the same time and his usual diuretics are withheld pending review.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98, BP 102/58, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 37.8
data_table.Examination: Tense ascites, generalised abdominal tenderness without guarding, no encephalopathy
data_table.Investigations: Ascitic neutrophils 480 x10^6/L; ascitic Gram stain negative; serum creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110); bilirubin 46 micromol/L (less than 20); international normalised ratio 1.5 (0.8-1.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral norfloxacin and repeat the paracentesis in 48 hours for cell count
options.rationale: Norfloxacin is the secondary prophylaxis agent given after an episode has been treated, not the treatment for an established infection with a raised neutrophil count (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start intravenous ceftriaxone and give intravenous albumin on days one and three
options.rationale: An ascitic neutrophil count of 250 x10^6/L or more defines spontaneous bacterial peritonitis regardless of culture, and albumin alongside the third generation cephalosporin reduces renal failure and mortality (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis).
source_refs: GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis

options.text: Await ascitic fluid culture results before committing to any antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Cultures are negative in about 40 per cent of true episodes, so the neutrophil count is the treatment trigger and waiting adds avoidable mortality (Source: GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis).
source_refs: GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis

options.text: Perform large volume paracentesis with albumin cover and restart both diuretics
options.rationale: Therapeutic drainage treats tense ascites but leaves the infection untreated, and reintroducing diuretics during sepsis risks precipitating renal impairment (Source: GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis).
source_refs: GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis

options.text: Start intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam and add oral metronidazole cover
options.rationale: Broad antipseudomonal cover with anaerobic doubling up is reserved for suspected secondary peritonitis from a perforated viscus, which the single organism picture here does not suggest (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Any patient with cirrhosis and ascites who deteriorates needs a diagnostic paracentesis before antibiotics, since the neutrophil count is the diagnostic test and it is degraded by prior treatment. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed at an ascitic neutrophil count of 250 x10^6/L or above, and culture negativity does not exclude it. Intravenous albumin at 1.5 g/kg on day one and 1 g/kg on day three reduces hepatorenal syndrome and death, with the greatest benefit in those with renal impairment or a bilirubin above 68 micromol/L. Survivors need indefinite secondary prophylaxis and assessment for liver transplantation.
key_points: Diagnostic paracentesis precedes antibiotics in any decompensating patient with ascites
Ascitic neutrophils of 250 x10^6/L or more diagnoses the infection whatever the culture shows
Third generation cephalosporin plus albumin is the treatment pair
Secondary prophylaxis with norfloxacin follows an episode, it does not treat one
Polymicrobial growth with a low glucose suggests secondary peritonitis needing imaging and surgery
explanation.pearls: Albumin is dosed at 1.5 g/kg within six hours of diagnosis and 1 g/kg on day three, and this pairing cuts mortality by roughly two thirds in patients with a creatinine above 88 micromol/L or bilirubin above 68 micromol/L.

sources.label: GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis

subtopic_detail: Albuminuric chronic kidney disease pharmacotherapy
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 61 year old man in the renal clinic. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension and takes perindopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily and metformin 1 g twice daily.

His blood pressure has been consistently below 130/80 at home and his glycaemic control has been stable for two years. Repeat urine testing over six months confirms persistent albuminuria and his estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 52 to 43 mL/min/1.73 m2 over eighteen months. Renal ultrasound shows two normal sized kidneys with no obstruction and his immunology screen is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 126/74, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: No peripheral oedema, no bruits, jugular venous pressure not elevated
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 43 mL/min/1.73 m2; urine albumin to creatinine ratio 48 mg/mmol (less than 2.5); potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); HbA1c 52 mmol/mol (less than 42)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next addition to his treatment?

options.text: Add candesartan to the perindopril and recheck the potassium in one week
options.rationale: Dual renin angiotensin blockade increases hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury without improving hard outcomes, and it was abandoned after the combination trials (Source: KHA-CARI Guidelines: Chronic Kidney Disease).

options.text: Add a thiazide diuretic and set a lower home blood pressure target of 120/70
options.rationale: His pressure is already at target, so further lowering treats a number that is not abnormal and does not address the albuminuria driving progression (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic Kidney Disease Management in Primary Care).
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic Kidney Disease Management in Primary Care

options.text: Stop metformin because of the falling filtration rate and start basal insulin
options.rationale: Metformin continues with dose review down to a filtration rate of 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, and stopping it here removes a well tolerated agent without protecting the kidney (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Add dapagliflozin and continue the current perindopril dose unchanged
options.rationale: A sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor added to maximally tolerated renin angiotensin blockade slows filtration rate decline and reduces kidney failure in albuminuric chronic kidney disease, independent of glycaemic effect (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic Kidney Disease Management in Primary Care; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic Kidney Disease Management in Primary Care

options.text: Add a low protein diet of 0.6 g/kg daily and review the ratio in six months
options.rationale: Severe protein restriction has modest and inconsistent benefit and risks malnutrition, so it does not displace an agent with randomised kidney outcome data (Source: KHA-CARI Guidelines: Chronic Kidney Disease).

explanation.summary: Chronic kidney disease risk is staged on the filtration rate and the albumin to creatinine ratio together, and this man sits in a high risk cell that warrants both nephrology involvement and drug escalation. The pillars of protection are a renin angiotensin blocker at the maximum tolerated dose, a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor, and in persisting albuminuria a non-steroidal mineralocorticoid antagonist such as finerenone. An expected early dip in filtration rate of up to 30 per cent after starting either class is haemodynamic and is not a reason to stop. Cardiovascular death remains a more likely outcome than dialysis at this stage, so lipid and blood pressure control run alongside.
key_points: Stage risk on filtration rate and albumin to creatinine ratio together, not filtration rate alone
Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors reduce kidney failure independent of glycaemic effect
An early filtration rate dip of up to 30 per cent is expected and not a stop signal
Dual renin angiotensin blockade is harmful and is not used
Metformin continues with dose review until the filtration rate falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2
explanation.pearls: Recheck the creatinine and potassium two to four weeks after starting dapagliflozin, and only investigate further if the filtration rate falls by more than 30 per cent from baseline.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic Kidney Disease Management in Primary Care

subtopic_detail: Treatment selection after minimal trauma vertebral fracture
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 72 year old woman four weeks after admission with sudden mid-back pain that began while she was hanging washing. Imaging showed a wedge compression fracture at T8 with no other cause identified.

She takes no glucocorticoids and has never smoked. Her bone mineral density scan shows a lumbar spine T-score of minus 2.1 and a femoral neck T-score of minus 2.3. She swallows tablets easily and can remain upright for half an hour after taking them.

data_table.Examination: Localised thoracic tenderness, no neurological deficit, height loss of 4 cm since age 60
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.60); 25-hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (more than 50); estimated glomerular filtration rate 74 mL/min/1.73 m2; thyroid function and serum protein electrophoresis within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment recommendation?

options.text: Advise calcium and vitamin D supplements with a supervised weight bearing program
options.rationale: Supplements and exercise support treatment but do not reduce refracture risk on their own after a vertebral fracture has already occurred (Source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis Management).
source_refs: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis Management

options.text: Start weekly oral alendronate with calcium and vitamin D intake reviewed
options.rationale: A minimal trauma vertebral fracture establishes osteoporosis regardless of the density result, and an oral bisphosphonate is the first line agent in a patient who can comply with dosing conditions (Source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis Management; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).
source_refs: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis Management

options.text: Defer drug treatment and repeat the density scan in two years to guide therapy
options.rationale: Refracture risk is highest in the two years after the index event, so deferral wastes the window in which treatment gives the largest absolute benefit (Source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis Management).
source_refs: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis Management

options.text: Start daily teriparatide injections as the initial agent for eighteen months
options.rationale: Anabolic therapy is restricted to very high risk disease with a T-score at or below minus 3.0 plus fractures on antiresorptive treatment, which she has not yet had (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Start six monthly denosumab injections and cease all other bone directed therapy
options.rationale: Denosumab is effective but is reserved for bisphosphonate intolerance or renal impairment, since missing a dose triggers rebound bone loss and vertebral fractures (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: A fracture from a fall at standing height or less in a person over 50 defines osteoporosis clinically, and treatment does not require a density result in the osteoporotic range. Before starting therapy, secondary causes are excluded with calcium, vitamin D, renal function, thyroid function and protein electrophoresis, and vitamin D is repleted so that antiresorptives do not precipitate hypocalcaemia. Oral bisphosphonates are first line, with intravenous zoledronic acid for those who cannot manage oral dosing conditions and denosumab where bisphosphonates are contraindicated. Treatment is reviewed after five years of oral therapy, with continuation in those who remain at high risk.
key_points: A minimal trauma fracture after age 50 diagnoses osteoporosis whatever the T-score
Exclude secondary causes and correct vitamin D before starting an antiresorptive
Oral bisphosphonate is first line; zoledronic acid suits those who cannot sit upright or swallow
Denosumab cannot simply be stopped because of rebound vertebral fracture risk
Refracture risk is concentrated in the first two years after the index fracture
explanation.pearls: Alendronate is taken on waking with a full glass of water, with the patient staying upright and fasted for at least 30 minutes, which is the single most common reason treatment fails in practice.

sources.label: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis Management

subtopic_detail: National bowel screening pathway after a positive immunochemical test
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a general medicine clinic seeing a 59 year old man who has brought in a letter reporting a positive result on his national bowel screening kit. He completed the kit six weeks ago after ignoring the previous two rounds.

He reports no change in bowel habit or rectal bleeding, and he feels entirely well. His father had a colonic polyp removed at age 70. He takes no regular medicines and has not previously been investigated.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no mass, rectal examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 146 g/L (130-175); ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30-300)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the immunochemical faecal test now and refer only if it is positive again
options.rationale: Repeating the test cannot lower the risk conferred by the positive result and simply delays the definitive investigation (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal Cancer Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Reassure him that a normal haemoglobin makes significant pathology very unlikely
options.rationale: Screen detected cancers are usually early and non-anaemic, so normal iron studies give false reassurance rather than a rule-out (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal Cancer Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Request computed tomography colonography as the initial diagnostic investigation
options.rationale: Computed tomography colonography is the alternative when colonoscopy is incomplete or contraindicated, because it cannot biopsy or remove a lesion (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal Cancer Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Refer for colonoscopy aiming for the procedure within 30 days of the result
options.rationale: A positive screening test carries roughly a one in twenty chance of cancer, and Australian guidance sets colonoscopy within 30 days as the target with 120 days the outer acceptable limit (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal Cancer Guidelines; National Bowel Cancer Screening Program).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Arrange carcinoembryonic antigen testing and refer if the level is above normal
options.rationale: Carcinoembryonic antigen is a postoperative surveillance marker with poor sensitivity for early disease and no role in triaging a positive screen (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal Cancer Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal Cancer Guidelines

explanation.summary: The Australian program mails an immunochemical faecal occult blood kit every two years to people aged 45 to 74, and a positive result is an indication for colonoscopy rather than for further stool testing. Absence of symptoms is expected in screen detected disease and does not modify the pathway. Timeliness matters because the risk of finding cancer rises with delay beyond four months from the positive result. Colonoscopy findings then determine surveillance intervals under the national polyp guidelines, and a normal colonoscopy returns the patient to routine screening after an interval.
key_points: The program screens ages 45 to 74 every two years with an immunochemical faecal test
A positive result means colonoscopy, not a repeat stool test
Target colonoscopy within 30 days and no later than 120 days from the result
About one in twenty positive results reflects a cancer and about one in three an advanced adenoma
Being asymptomatic and non-anaemic does not modify the pathway
explanation.pearls: Colonoscopy delayed beyond 120 days after a positive immunochemical faecal test is associated with a measurable rise in the proportion of cancers found at an advanced stage, which is why the 30 day target exists.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal Cancer Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Anticipatory prescribing for breathlessness at the end of life
stem:
You are the medical registrar caring for a 76 year old woman with metastatic lung cancer who has chosen to die at home with community palliative care support. Disease directed treatment was stopped three weeks ago and she is now bed bound and drowsy for much of the day.

She describes distressing breathlessness at rest that is worst when she is repositioned. Oxygen saturation is 94 per cent on room air and a trial of a handheld fan gave only partial relief. She has no history of opioid use, her renal function is preserved and the family asks what they should have at home for the coming days.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 106/64, RR 26, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Reduced air entry at the right base, no wheeze, no peripheral oedema, chest wall not tender
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL/min/1.73 m2; haemoglobin 112 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prescription for her breathlessness?

options.text: Low dose immediate release oral morphine regularly with breakthrough doses available
options.rationale: Regular low dose opioid is the best evidenced pharmacological treatment for refractory breathlessness in advanced disease and works without depending on the oxygen saturation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care; CareSearch Palliative Care Knowledge Network).

options.text: Continuous home oxygen by nasal prongs titrated to comfort during repositioning
options.rationale: Oxygen benefits hypoxaemic patients, and at a saturation of 94 per cent it performs no better than airflow from a fan while adding equipment burden at home (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care).

options.text: Regular oral diazepam with additional doses available for episodic distress
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are second line and are added for anxiety that persists despite an opioid, since alone they do not reduce the sensation of breathlessness (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care).

options.text: Regular nebulised salbutamol four times daily with saline nebulisers in between
options.rationale: Bronchodilators help only when reversible airflow obstruction is present, and she has no wheeze to support that mechanism (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Regular oral dexamethasone with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
options.rationale: Corticosteroid targets lymphangitis or airway compression rather than the general breathlessness of advanced disease, and carries delirium and myopathy risk at this stage (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care).

explanation.summary: Refractory breathlessness in advanced disease is treated first with non-drug measures such as airflow from a fan, positioning and breathing techniques, then with regular low dose opioid. Doses used for breathlessness are lower than analgesic doses and are titrated slowly, and there is no evidence that careful titration hastens death. Anticipatory prescribing means leaving a small stock of subcutaneous medicines in the home so the family and visiting nurses can treat breathlessness, pain, nausea, secretions and agitation without waiting for a new script. Reversible contributors such as effusion, anaemia, infection and pulmonary embolism are considered first if the burden of investigation is proportionate.
key_points: Non-drug measures including a handheld fan come first and continue alongside drugs
Regular low dose opioid is the primary pharmacological treatment for refractory breathlessness
Oxygen helps only when the patient is hypoxaemic
Benzodiazepines are second line for persisting anxiety on top of an opioid
Anticipatory subcutaneous medicines cover breathlessness, pain, nausea, secretions and agitation
explanation.pearls: Opioid naive patients start at about 2.5 mg immediate release oral morphine every four hours with breakthrough doses, roughly a quarter to a third of typical analgesic starting doses, and are reviewed after 48 hours.

subtopic_detail: Obstructive sleep apnoea and fitness to drive
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 48 year old man who drives a semi-trailer interstate and holds a commercial licence. His partner reports loud snoring with witnessed pauses, and he describes falling asleep at traffic lights twice in the past month.

His body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and his Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 17 out of 24. A laboratory sleep study performed last week reports an apnoea hypopnoea index of 42 events per hour with oxygen desaturation to 84 per cent. His thyroid function and morning cortisol are within normal limits and he takes no sedating medicines.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 148/88, RR 14, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Neck circumference 46 cm, Mallampati class 4, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Apnoea hypopnoea index 42 events per hour; nadir oxygen saturation 84 per cent; HbA1c 44 mmol/mol (less than 42)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Start continuous positive airway pressure and clear him to keep driving meanwhile
options.rationale: Starting treatment does not immediately remove the crash risk, and letting him continue commercial driving while he is falling asleep at the wheel ignores the standard (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).

options.text: Recommend a six month supervised weight loss program before any device therapy
options.rationale: Weight loss is important adjunctive therapy but is far too slow to address severe disease with documented sleepiness at the wheel (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea

options.text: Advise him not to drive, notify the licensing authority, and start airway pressure therapy
options.rationale: Severe disease with sleepiness at the wheel makes a commercial driver unfit until treated, and Australian standards require the treating doctor to advise cessation and support reporting to the driver licensing authority (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive; Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea

options.text: Fit a mandibular advancement splint and repeat the sleep study in three months
options.rationale: Oral appliances are an option for mild to moderate disease or airway pressure intolerance, and are unreliable at an index above 30 events per hour (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea

options.text: Prescribe modafinil for daytime sleepiness and review his symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Wake promoting agents are only considered for residual sleepiness on adherent airway pressure therapy, and masking sleepiness in an untreated driver is the anti-pattern here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea is graded by the apnoea hypopnoea index as mild at 5 to 15, moderate at 15 to 30 and severe above 30 events per hour, and treatment decisions combine that index with daytime symptoms and comorbidity. Continuous positive airway pressure is first line in severe disease, with oral appliances and weight management as alternatives or adjuncts in milder disease. Fitness to drive is assessed against the Australian commercial and private standards, which are stricter for commercial licence holders and hinge on both the severity of disease and on documented sleepiness or a sleep related crash. Once treated and adherent with resolution of sleepiness, a conditional commercial licence can be granted with annual review.
key_points: An apnoea hypopnoea index above 30 events per hour is severe disease
Airway pressure therapy is first line in severe disease and in commercial drivers
Falling asleep at the wheel makes a commercial driver unfit until treated
Doctors advise the patient not to drive and support notification of the licensing authority
Conditional commercial licensing follows documented adherence and symptom resolution
explanation.pearls: Commercial licence holders need documented device adherence, usually at least four hours nightly on 70 per cent of nights, plus resolution of daytime sleepiness before a conditional licence with annual review is granted.

sources.label: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea

subtopic_detail: Severe cutaneous adverse reaction discrimination
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 63 year old man with a widespread rash and fever. He began allopurinol 24 days ago after two attacks of gout and takes perindopril unchanged for six years.

He has a confluent red rash over more than half his body surface with marked swelling of his face and eyelids. There is no mucosal ulceration, no blistering and Nikolsky sign is negative. He has palpable cervical lymph nodes and mild right upper quadrant discomfort.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106, BP 128/74, RR 20, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption with facial oedema, cervical lymphadenopathy, mucosae intact
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5); alanine aminotransferase 216 U/L (less than 40); creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110); atypical lymphocytes on film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Transfer to a burns unit for management of extensive epidermal detachment
options.rationale: Burns unit transfer is driven by epidermal detachment and mucosal involvement, and a negative Nikolsky sign with intact mucosae points away from that diagnosis (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions).
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Continue allopurinol, give oral antihistamines, and review the rash in 48 hours
options.rationale: Antihistamines treat urticaria and do nothing for a T cell mediated systemic reaction, and continuing the culprit drug drives ongoing organ injury (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions).
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Cease perindopril as the likely culprit and observe on antihistamines overnight
options.rationale: A drug taken unchanged for six years is a poor fit for a reaction with a two to eight week latency, whereas allopurinol started 24 days ago fits precisely (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions).
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Start intravenous immunoglobulin and admit for continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is debated in toxic epidermal necrolysis and has no established role in this eosinophilic multi-organ reaction, where corticosteroid is standard (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Drug Hypersensitivity Syndromes).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Drug Hypersensitivity Syndromes

options.text: Cease allopurinol immediately and start systemic corticosteroid with organ monitoring
options.rationale: The latency, facial oedema, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes and hepatic plus renal involvement identify a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, treated by stopping the culprit and giving systemic corticosteroid with staged organ surveillance (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions; Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is separated from Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis by its long latency of two to eight weeks, facial oedema, eosinophilia with atypical lymphocytes and prominent internal organ involvement with largely intact mucosae. Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline are the classic culprits. Liver injury is the commonest organ manifestation, but myocarditis and thyroiditis can appear weeks to months later, so surveillance continues after the rash resolves. Relapse on steroid weaning is common and viral reactivation, particularly human herpesvirus 6, is implicated in the prolonged course.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks separates this reaction from an ordinary drug exanthem
Facial oedema, eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes with intact mucosae are the signature
Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides and vancomycin are the usual culprits
Liver is the commonest organ involved; myocarditis and thyroiditis can present late
Treatment is culprit withdrawal plus systemic corticosteroid with a slow wean
explanation.pearls: Thyroid function is rechecked at about three months after this reaction because autoimmune thyroiditis appears well after the rash has cleared and is missed if surveillance stops at discharge.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions
BMJ Best Practice: Drug Hypersensitivity Syndromes

subtopic_detail: Parkinsonism with hallucinations and antipsychotic selection
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 74 year old man admitted with a fall. His wife reports that for eight months he has seen small animals in the lounge room in the late afternoon, and that on some days he is sharp and on others barely rouses from his chair.

He was started on metoclopramide seven weeks ago for reflux. Cognitive testing shows impaired attention and visuospatial function with relatively preserved recall. Examination shows symmetric bradykinesia with mild rigidity and no tremor, and his wife adds that for several years he has shouted and thrashed during dreams. He has had no urinary symptoms and postural blood pressures show no significant drop.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, no resting tremor, gait short stepped, no cerebellar signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function, calcium, thyroid function and B12 within normal limits; computed tomography brain shows mild generalised atrophy only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his hallucinations?

options.text: Start risperidone 0.5 mg at night and review his symptoms in one week
options.rationale: Antipsychotics with strong dopamine blockade can cause a severe sensitivity reaction with rigidity and collapse in this condition, and risperidone is among the worst offenders (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start levodopa with carbidopa and continue the metoclopramide for his reflux
options.rationale: Dopaminergic therapy may be needed later for motor symptoms, but starting it while a dopamine antagonist continues is self-defeating and can worsen hallucinations (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Start donepezil and add regular oxazepam at night for behavioural disturbance
options.rationale: A cholinesterase inhibitor is reasonable therapy here, but pairing it with a regular benzodiazepine adds falls and confusion in a man already presenting after a fall (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start quetiapine 25 mg at night and continue the metoclopramide for his reflux
options.rationale: Quetiapine is the least harmful antipsychotic if one is unavoidable, but reaching for it before removing an offending dopamine antagonist treats the symptom and leaves the cause (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease metoclopramide, treat reversible contributors, and start a cholinesterase inhibitor
options.rationale: Fluctuating attention, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and a long standing dream enactment history indicate Lewy body disease, where the first moves are withdrawing dopamine antagonists and treating with a cholinesterase inhibitor rather than an antipsychotic (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; Dementia Australia Clinical Practice Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies is defined by fluctuating cognition, recurrent well formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism and rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, the last of which often precedes cognitive change by years. Severe antipsychotic sensitivity occurs in up to half of patients and can be fatal, so drugs with potent dopamine blockade including metoclopramide and prochlorperazine are avoided entirely. Cholinesterase inhibitors have better evidence for hallucinations and cognition here than in Alzheimer disease. Levodopa may be used cautiously for disabling motor symptoms but is titrated slowly because it can aggravate psychosis.
key_points: Dream enactment behaviour often precedes cognitive decline by years and is a strong pointer
Cognitive fluctuation with impaired attention and visuospatial function distinguishes it from Alzheimer disease
Metoclopramide and prochlorperazine cause drug induced parkinsonism and are ceased first
Antipsychotic sensitivity reactions occur in up to half of patients and can be fatal
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first line for hallucinations and cognitive symptoms
explanation.pearls: If an antipsychotic is genuinely unavoidable in Lewy body disease, quetiapine at 12.5 to 25 mg at night is the least harmful choice, and any rigidity or fever after a dose is treated as a sensitivity reaction until proven otherwise.

subtopic_detail: Deteriorating myasthenia gravis and respiratory assessment
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 38 year old woman with acetylcholine receptor antibody positive myasthenia gravis, admitted with four days of worsening weakness after a urinary tract infection treated with nitrofurantoin. She takes pyridostigmine 60 mg five times daily and prednisolone 15 mg daily.

She can no longer lift her head from the pillow and her speech becomes unintelligible after two sentences. She has no muscarinic features such as cramps or excess salivation, and her pupils are 3 mm and reactive. Forced vital capacity measured at the bedside is 1.1 L, having been 2.2 L on admission, and her single breath count is 12.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 138/82, RR 24, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.2
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, weak neck flexion, nasal speech, paradoxical abdominal movement when supine
data_table.Investigations: Arterial blood gas on room air pH 7.42, PaCO2 41 mmHg (35-45), PaO2 84 mmHg (80-100), bicarbonate 25 mmol/L (22-32)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase pyridostigmine to 90 mg five times daily and reassess in four hours
options.rationale: Escalating cholinesterase inhibition adds secretions without reversing the immunological crisis, and it delays the definitive treatment while her vital capacity falls (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Withhold pyridostigmine and give intravenous atropine for cholinergic excess
options.rationale: Cholinergic crisis is the near-pair diagnosis but requires muscarinic overactivity with cramps, diarrhoea, salivation and small pupils, none of which she has (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Myasthenia Gravis).

options.text: Arrange critical care review for airway support and start immunoglobulin or plasma exchange
options.rationale: A halving of forced vital capacity to about 15 mL/kg with bulbar weakness is impending neuromuscular respiratory failure, so critical care involvement precedes any gas abnormality and rapid acting immunotherapy is started (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; BMJ Best Practice: Myasthenia Gravis).

options.text: Start high flow nasal oxygen and repeat the arterial blood gas in two hours
options.rationale: Oxygen corrects the number while masking rising carbon dioxide, and in neuromuscular weakness the gas is normal until immediately before collapse (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Myasthenia Gravis).

options.text: Increase prednisolone to 50 mg daily and continue current ward level observation
options.rationale: High dose corticosteroid transiently worsens weakness in the first one to two weeks, so it is added under cover of immunoglobulin or exchange rather than used alone in a crisis (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is respiratory or bulbar failure severe enough to need ventilatory support, and it is most often precipitated by infection, surgery, pregnancy or a drug such as an aminoglycoside, fluoroquinolone, macrolide or magnesium. Bedside forced vital capacity and single breath count track the trajectory far better than oxygen saturation or arterial gases, both of which stay reassuring until decompensation. Definitive treatment is intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, with corticosteroid escalation covered by that rapid acting therapy because steroids transiently worsen weakness. Cholinergic crisis from excessive pyridostigmine is the classic mimic but is now rare and requires muscarinic features to be diagnosed.
key_points: Serial forced vital capacity and single breath count guide escalation, not oxygen saturation
A vital capacity below about 15 to 20 mL/kg predicts the need for ventilatory support
Normal arterial carbon dioxide does not exclude impending neuromuscular respiratory failure
Immunoglobulin and plasma exchange work equally quickly; choice depends on access and comorbidity
Cholinergic crisis needs muscarinic features such as cramps, diarrhoea, salivation and small pupils
explanation.pearls: Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, magnesium and beta blockers all worsen neuromuscular transmission, and a single dose of intravenous magnesium for another indication can precipitate crisis in a stable myasthenic patient.

subtopic_detail: Early Guillain-Barre spectrum with non-diagnostic cerebrospinal fluid
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 29 year old man with three days of unsteadiness and double vision. Ten days ago he had a diarrhoeal illness after a barbecue that settled without treatment.

He walks with a broad based gait and cannot tandem walk. He has bilateral partial external ophthalmoplegia, absent ankle and knee reflexes, and normal power in all limbs. Sensation to pinprick and vibration is intact, with no sensory level and no back pain. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and whole spine is normal, and the cerebrospinal fluid taken today shows protein 0.38 g/L with one white cell.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 126/76, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ophthalmoplegia, areflexia, ataxic gait, power 5/5 throughout, no sensory level
data_table.Investigations: Cerebrospinal fluid protein 0.38 g/L (0.15-0.45); cerebrospinal fluid white cells 1 x10^6/L (less than 5); forced vital capacity 3.6 L; glucose and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat the lumbar puncture in seven days and withhold treatment until protein rises
options.rationale: Protein does rise in the second week, but withholding immunotherapy to wait for a confirmatory number risks progression during the treatment window (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Start intravenous immunoglobulin and monitor vital capacity and swallowing
options.rationale: Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia after a diarrhoeal illness is a Guillain-Barre spectrum presentation, and normal early cerebrospinal fluid protein does not exclude it because the rise lags the first week (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; BMJ Best Practice: Guillain-Barre Syndrome).

options.text: Give intravenous methylprednisolone for three days and arrange neurology review
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are ineffective in this condition and were shown not to speed recovery, which separates it from the inflammatory demyelinating conditions where they work (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Guillain-Barre Syndrome).

options.text: Give intravenous thiamine and treat for a nutritional brainstem syndrome
options.rationale: Thiamine deficiency gives ophthalmoplegia and ataxia but with confusion and preserved reflexes, and there is no nutritional risk history here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography angiography of the posterior circulation
options.rationale: Brainstem ischaemia is the reflex worry with ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, but generalised areflexia and a normal magnetic resonance scan point away from a vascular lesion (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Guillain-Barre Syndrome).

explanation.summary: The Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome presents with the triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia, frequently after Campylobacter jejuni enteritis, and is associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies. Albuminocytological dissociation is present in fewer than half of patients in the first week, so a normal cerebrospinal fluid protein early in the illness carries little weight against the clinical picture. Treatment is intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, and corticosteroids do not help. Monitoring focuses on vital capacity, bulbar function and autonomic instability, since these determine whether critical care is required rather than limb power.
key_points: Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia define the Miller Fisher variant
Cerebrospinal fluid protein is often normal in the first week and rises in the second
Campylobacter jejuni is the classic antecedent infection
Immunoglobulin or plasma exchange are effective; corticosteroids are not
Vital capacity, bulbar function and autonomic instability drive escalation decisions
explanation.pearls: Anti-GQ1b antibodies are positive in over 85 per cent of Miller Fisher cases, but treatment starts on clinical grounds because the assay usually takes days to return.

subtopic_detail: Acute kidney injury in decompensated cirrhosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 54 year old woman with hepatitis C related cirrhosis and diuretic controlled ascites, admitted five days ago with peritonitis that is now improving on ceftriaxone. Her diuretics were stopped on admission.

Her creatinine has risen from a baseline of 74 micromol/L to 196 micromol/L despite 48 hours of intravenous albumin at 1 g/kg daily. She has passed 380 mL of urine in the last 24 hours. She has received no contrast and no nephrotoxic drug, and renal ultrasound shows normal sized unobstructed kidneys.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 92/54, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Moderate ascites, warm peripheries, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no asterixis
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 196 micromol/L (45-90); sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145); urinary sodium 8 mmol/L; urine microscopy shows no casts and no protein; ascitic neutrophils now 90 x10^6/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give a 1 litre crystalloid bolus and repeat the creatinine in six hours
options.rationale: Crystalloid distributes into the ascitic compartment and does not expand the effective circulating volume the way albumin does, so it is not the volume challenge used here (Source: GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis).
source_refs: GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis

options.text: Restart frusemide and spironolactone to control the ascites and improve output
options.rationale: Diuretics are withheld during acute kidney injury in cirrhosis because further volume depletion is one of the commonest precipitants (Source: GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis).
source_refs: GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis

options.text: Change ceftriaxone to meropenem and continue supportive care unchanged
options.rationale: The ascitic neutrophil count has fallen, indicating the infection is responding, so broadening cover addresses a problem that has already resolved (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start terlipressin with continued albumin and refer for transplantation assessment
options.rationale: Failure to respond to 48 hours of albumin with diuretic withdrawal, a bland urinary sediment and a urinary sodium below 20 mmol/L defines hepatorenal acute kidney injury, treated with a vasoconstrictor plus albumin while transplant assessment proceeds (Source: GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis; BMJ Best Practice: Hepatorenal Syndrome).
source_refs: GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis

options.text: Arrange urgent renal biopsy to distinguish tubular necrosis from glomerular disease
options.rationale: Biopsy carries substantial bleeding risk in coagulopathy and ascites, and the bland sediment with very low urinary sodium already argues against intrinsic renal disease (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hepatorenal Syndrome).

explanation.summary: Acute kidney injury complicates about one in five hospital admissions in cirrhosis, and the differential is prerenal from volume depletion, acute tubular necrosis and hepatorenal physiology from splanchnic vasodilatation with intense renal vasoconstriction. The diagnostic step is the same for all three: stop diuretics and nephrotoxins, exclude obstruction and infection, and give albumin at 1 g/kg daily for two days. Persisting injury after that challenge with a bland sediment and avid sodium retention is hepatorenal, which responds to splanchnic vasoconstriction with terlipressin or noradrenaline plus albumin. Because the underlying liver disease is what drives it, transplantation assessment runs in parallel and is the only definitive treatment.
key_points: Stop diuretics and nephrotoxins and give albumin 1 g/kg daily for two days as the diagnostic challenge
Bland urinary sediment with urinary sodium below 20 mmol/L supports hepatorenal physiology
Terlipressin with albumin is the pharmacological treatment; noradrenaline is the critical care alternative
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is a major precipitant, which is why albumin is given at diagnosis
Transplantation assessment proceeds in parallel because it is the only definitive treatment
explanation.pearls: Terlipressin causes ischaemic complications in about 10 per cent of patients, so peripheral perfusion and any history of coronary or peripheral vascular disease are checked before the first dose and daily during treatment.

sources.label: GESA Ascites and Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis

subtopic_detail: Effusion classification in a diuretic treated patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 79 year old woman with known heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, admitted three days ago with breathlessness and treated with intravenous frusemide. She has lost 4 kg and her breathlessness has improved, but a right sided effusion persists on chest radiograph.

She has never smoked and reports no chest pain or fever, with no occupational asbestos exposure. A diagnostic pleural aspiration is performed today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80, BP 118/70, RR 18, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Stony dull percussion to mid zone on the right, jugular venous pressure 3 cm, trace ankle oedema
data_table.Investigations: Pleural protein 32 g/L; serum protein 68 g/L; pleural lactate dehydrogenase 168 U/L; serum lactate dehydrogenase 250 U/L; pleural albumin 21 g/L; serum albumin 36 g/L; pleural glucose and pH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Treat as a transudate given the albumin gradient and continue heart failure therapy
options.rationale: Diuresis concentrates pleural protein and pushes a transudate across the Light criteria threshold, and a serum to pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L correctly reclassifies it as a transudate (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural Disease; BMJ Best Practice: Pleural Effusion).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural Disease

options.text: Treat as an exudate by the protein ratio and arrange contrast computed tomography
options.rationale: The protein ratio of 0.47 does exceed the Light threshold, but applying the criteria uncritically after diuresis is the classic misclassification this scenario tests (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Pleural Effusion).

options.text: Insert an intercostal catheter for drainage and send fluid for cytological analysis
options.rationale: Tube drainage is for infected or symptomatic large effusions, and neither the normal pleural pH nor her improving symptoms support it (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural Disease).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural Disease

options.text: Refer for thoracoscopy with pleural biopsy to exclude malignant pleural disease
options.rationale: Thoracoscopy is reserved for an undiagnosed exudate after negative cytology, so it skips two steps once the fluid is correctly classified (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural Disease).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural Disease

options.text: Start empirical antibiotics for parapneumonic infection and repeat the aspiration
options.rationale: Pleural infection requires a low pleural pH, low glucose or organisms on Gram stain, and she is afebrile with normal fluid chemistry (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Light criteria classify an effusion as exudative if the pleural to serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5, the pleural to serum lactate dehydrogenase ratio exceeds 0.6, or pleural lactate dehydrogenase exceeds two thirds of the upper limit of the serum reference range. The criteria are highly sensitive for exudates but misclassify around a quarter of transudates as exudates in patients who have received diuretics, because water is removed faster than protein. When the clinical picture says transudate and the criteria say exudate, the serum to pleural albumin gradient resolves the conflict, with a value above 12 g/L indicating a transudate. Misclassification matters because it sends a patient with heart failure down an invasive investigation pathway.
key_points: Light criteria are sensitive for exudates but misclassify diuresed transudates
A serum to pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L indicates a transudate
A serum to pleural protein gradient above 31 g/L is the alternative reclassifying test
Pleural pH below 7.2 in a parapneumonic effusion indicates the need for drainage
Undiagnosed exudates after negative cytology proceed to thoracoscopic biopsy
explanation.pearls: Send serum protein, albumin and lactate dehydrogenase at the same time as the pleural tap, because the gradients cannot be calculated retrospectively if the bloods were taken on a different day of diuresis.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural Disease

subtopic_detail: Major bleeding on a factor Xa inhibitor
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department for a 77 year old man with atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily who has vomited fresh blood twice in the past hour. His last apixaban dose was six hours ago.

He is pale and clammy with ongoing haematemesis in the department. He takes no antiplatelet agent and has had no previous ulcer. Two units of red cells have been started and the gastroenterology on call has been contacted for urgent endoscopy. His renal function is preserved and there is no prior history of thrombosis beyond the atrial fibrillation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 84/52, RR 24, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.2
data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries, epigastric tenderness, melaena on rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 71 g/L (130-175); platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110); international normalised ratio 1.3 (0.8-1.2); fibrinogen 2.4 g/L (2.0-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate haemostatic intervention?

options.text: Give prothrombin complex concentrate alongside resuscitation and urgent endoscopy
options.rationale: Prothrombin complex concentrate is the Australian standard reversal for life threatening factor Xa inhibitor bleeding when a specific antidote is unavailable, and it is given while the source is controlled endoscopically (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Give intravenous vitamin K 10 mg and fresh frozen plasma while awaiting endoscopy
options.rationale: Vitamin K and plasma reverse warfarin by replacing carboxylated factors, but neither displaces a direct factor Xa inhibitor from its target (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Give intravenous protamine sulfate and repeat the coagulation profile in one hour
options.rationale: Protamine neutralises heparins by ionic binding and has no activity against oral factor Xa inhibitors (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Give idarucizumab as a 5 g intravenous dose and proceed to urgent endoscopy
options.rationale: Idarucizumab is the monoclonal antibody fragment specific to dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, and it does not bind apixaban (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Give activated charcoal by nasogastric tube and withhold further anticoagulation
options.rationale: Charcoal only helps within about two to four hours of ingestion, and passing a nasogastric tube during active haematemesis adds risk without haemostatic benefit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

explanation.summary: Reversal decisions in anticoagulant associated bleeding depend on identifying the drug class, the time since the last dose and the severity of bleeding. Dabigatran has a specific antidote in idarucizumab and is also dialysable, while factor Xa inhibitors are reversed with prothrombin complex concentrate in Australian practice, with andexanet alfa restricted in availability. Standard coagulation tests are unreliable for direct oral anticoagulants, since a normal international normalised ratio does not exclude a therapeutic drug level. Resuscitation, transfusion and definitive source control run in parallel with any haemostatic agent, and the timing of anticoagulant restart is a separate decision made once haemostasis is secure.
key_points: Identify the anticoagulant class before choosing a reversal agent
Prothrombin complex concentrate is the Australian reversal option for factor Xa inhibitor bleeding
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only; dabigatran is also dialysable
Vitamin K and plasma reverse warfarin, not direct oral anticoagulants
A normal international normalised ratio does not exclude therapeutic anticoagulant levels
explanation.pearls: Prothrombin complex concentrate for factor Xa inhibitor bleeding is dosed at about 50 units/kg, and the anticoagulant is not restarted until haemostasis has held, usually reconsidered within the first week to limit stroke risk.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulant choice in cancer associated thrombosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to advise on anticoagulation for a 66 year old woman with a newly diagnosed locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma who has a confirmed segmental pulmonary embolism on computed tomography. She is haemodynamically stable and is due to start chemotherapy next week.

She describes intermittent nausea with reduced oral intake and has had two episodes of small volume coffee ground vomiting in the past fortnight. Her endoscopy report describes a friable ulcerated tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction. Renal function is preserved and she takes no antiplatelet drug.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 118/72, RR 20, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: No leg swelling, chest clear, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155); platelets 240 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 76 micromol/L (45-90); right ventricular size normal on computed tomography

lead_in: Which anticoagulation strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Oral rivaroxaban at treatment dose continued for at least six months
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are acceptable in many cancers but carry excess major bleeding when the tumour is an intact luminal gastrointestinal lesion (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Venous Thromboembolism in Cancer).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Venous Thromboembolism in Cancer

options.text: Warfarin bridged with enoxaparin, targeting an international normalised ratio of 2 to 3
options.rationale: Vitamin K antagonists perform worse than low molecular weight heparin in cancer because appetite, vomiting and chemotherapy interactions make control erratic (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Venous Thromboembolism in Cancer).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Venous Thromboembolism in Cancer

options.text: Retrievable inferior vena cava filter with no systemic anticoagulation started
options.rationale: Filters are for absolute contraindications to anticoagulation, and coffee ground vomiting without active haemorrhage does not meet that bar (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Prophylactic dose enoxaparin daily with weekly review through chemotherapy
options.rationale: Prophylactic dosing does not treat established embolism, and undertreating an event carries a high early recurrence risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Therapeutic dose enoxaparin daily, reviewed as treatment and bleeding risk evolve
options.rationale: Low molecular weight heparin remains preferred when a luminal gastrointestinal tumour and recent upper gastrointestinal blood loss raise direct oral anticoagulant bleeding risk, and it can be held easily around procedures (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Venous Thromboembolism in Cancer; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Venous Thromboembolism in Cancer

explanation.summary: Cancer associated thrombosis carries both a higher recurrence risk and a higher bleeding risk than thrombosis in other patients, so agent selection weighs the two against the tumour site. Direct oral anticoagulants are now first line for most cancers, but randomised data show excess major gastrointestinal bleeding with edoxaban and rivaroxaban when there is an intact luminal gastrointestinal or genitourinary tumour. Low molecular weight heparin is preferred in that setting and where vomiting, mucositis or drug interactions make absorption unreliable. Anticoagulation continues for at least six months and then for as long as the cancer is active or treatment continues, with periodic reassessment of platelet count and bleeding risk.
key_points: Cancer associated thrombosis has higher recurrence and higher bleeding risk than other thrombosis
Luminal gastrointestinal and genitourinary tumours shift the choice away from oral factor Xa inhibitors
Low molecular weight heparin suits unreliable absorption and frequent procedural interruptions
Vitamin K antagonists are a poor choice because of erratic control during chemotherapy
Treat for at least six months and continue while the cancer is active
explanation.pearls: When the platelet count falls between 25 and 50 x10^9/L during chemotherapy, halve the therapeutic low molecular weight heparin dose rather than stopping it, and withhold entirely below 25 x10^9/L.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Venous Thromboembolism in Cancer

subtopic_detail: Menopausal hormone therapy regimen selection
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 52 year old woman whose last menstrual period was eighteen months ago. She has fifteen to twenty hot flushes a day and wakes drenched three or four times a night, and she has stopped attending her book club because of them.

Her uterus is intact and a recent transvaginal ultrasound for a single episode of spotting showed an endometrial thickness of 3 mm. She has no personal or family history of breast cancer and no history of venous thromboembolism. Her blood pressure is well controlled on no medication and she has tried an eight week trial of a serotonin reuptake inhibitor with little benefit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 124/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, breast examination normal, no pelvic mass
data_table.Investigations: Endometrial thickness 3 mm on transvaginal ultrasound; cervical screening up to date and negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to recommend?

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol alone applied twice weekly with annual pelvic ultrasound
options.rationale: Unopposed oestrogen in a woman with a uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma, and surveillance scanning does not substitute for progestogen protection (Source: RANZCOG: Menopausal Hormone Therapy).

options.text: Cyclical oestradiol with a twelve day progestogen to produce a monthly bleed
options.rationale: Sequential regimens suit the perimenopause, and reintroducing a monthly bleed eighteen months after the final period is unnecessary (Source: RANZCOG: Menopausal Hormone Therapy).

options.text: Continuous combined transdermal oestradiol with oral micronised progesterone
options.rationale: More than twelve months past the final period a continuous combined regimen avoids scheduled bleeding, and transdermal oestradiol with micronised progesterone carries the most favourable thrombotic and breast profile (Source: RANZCOG: Menopausal Hormone Therapy; Australasian Menopause Society).

options.text: Tibolone daily with review of vasomotor symptoms after three months of therapy
options.rationale: Tibolone is a reasonable alternative but is second line, with less symptom efficacy and a stroke signal in women over 60 (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

options.text: Vaginal oestradiol pessaries twice weekly with a non-hormonal oral adjunct
options.rationale: Low dose vaginal oestrogen treats genitourinary symptoms and achieves negligible systemic levels, so it does not relieve vasomotor symptoms (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

explanation.summary: Menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and is appropriate for healthy symptomatic women under 60 or within ten years of their final period. Women with a uterus need a progestogen to protect the endometrium, given sequentially in the perimenopause and continuously once more than twelve months past the final period. Transdermal oestradiol avoids first pass metabolism and is not associated with the venous thromboembolism excess seen with oral preparations, making it preferred in women with obesity, migraine or thrombotic risk. Micronised progesterone appears to carry a lower breast cancer signal than synthetic progestogens and is better tolerated in terms of mood.
key_points: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms
A uterus means a progestogen is mandatory, sequential before and continuous after twelve months of amenorrhoea
Transdermal oestradiol avoids the venous thromboembolism excess of oral preparations
Micronised progesterone has the most favourable breast and metabolic profile
Vaginal oestrogen treats genitourinary symptoms only and does not need systemic progestogen cover
explanation.pearls: Unscheduled bleeding in the first six months of continuous combined therapy is common and observed, but bleeding persisting beyond six months or starting after amenorrhoea has been established requires endometrial assessment.

subtopic_detail: Genitourinary symptoms after hormone receptor positive breast cancer
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58 year old woman referred with vaginal dryness and pain with penetration that has worsened over a year. She finished treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer three years ago and is in year three of anastrozole with two years remaining.

She has tried a lubricant at intercourse only, with little benefit. She has no bleeding or discharge. Examination shows pale thin vaginal walls with loss of rugae, and her most recent oncology review was clear.

data_table.Examination: Pale atrophic vaginal epithelium, loss of rugae, no lesion or ulceration, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus; vaginal swab shows no infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Vaginal oestriol cream three nights weekly after discussion with her oncologist
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen is considered only after non-hormonal measures fail, and on an aromatase inhibitor it requires an explicit shared decision because even minimal absorption is contentious (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause).
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause

options.text: Systemic transdermal oestradiol with oral micronised progesterone protection
options.rationale: Systemic hormone therapy is contraindicated after hormone receptor positive breast cancer and would directly oppose her endocrine treatment (Source: RANZCOG: Menopausal Hormone Therapy).

options.text: Regular vaginal moisturiser with lubricant at intercourse and pelvic floor physiotherapy
options.rationale: Non-hormonal moisturisers used regularly rather than only at intercourse, combined with pelvic floor physiotherapy for the secondary muscle response, is the first line approach in women who cannot use oestrogen (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause; Cancer Australia: Managing Menopausal Symptoms after Breast Cancer).
