source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause
Cancer Australia: Managing Menopausal Symptoms after Breast Cancer

options.text: Switch anastrozole to tamoxifen to improve her vaginal symptoms during treatment
options.rationale: Changing adjuvant endocrine therapy for a symptom is an oncology decision with survival implications, and tamoxifen brings its own vaginal and endometrial effects (Source: Cancer Australia: Managing Menopausal Symptoms after Breast Cancer).
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Managing Menopausal Symptoms after Breast Cancer

options.text: Fractional carbon dioxide laser therapy delivered as three treatments six weeks apart
options.rationale: Sham controlled trials have not shown benefit over placebo, and the therapy is not recommended outside research settings (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause).
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause

explanation.summary: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause is progressive and does not remit spontaneously, unlike vasomotor symptoms. Aromatase inhibitors profoundly suppress oestrogen and commonly produce severe symptoms that threaten adherence to adjuvant therapy, so active management protects cancer outcomes as well as quality of life. First line care is regular vaginal moisturisers used two or three times weekly independent of sexual activity, lubricants at intercourse, and pelvic floor physiotherapy where there is secondary pelvic floor overactivity. Low dose vaginal oestrogen is reserved for refractory symptoms and, on an aromatase inhibitor, is used only after discussion with the treating oncologist.
key_points: Genitourinary syndrome is progressive and needs ongoing rather than episodic treatment
Moisturisers are used regularly, not just at intercourse; lubricants are used at intercourse
Pelvic floor physiotherapy addresses the secondary overactivity that maintains pain
Low dose vaginal oestrogen is second line and needs oncology input on an aromatase inhibitor
Vaginal laser therapy has not outperformed sham in randomised trials
explanation.pearls: Aromatase inhibitor associated vaginal symptoms are a leading cause of early discontinuation of adjuvant endocrine therapy, and treating them well is a recognised way of protecting five year adherence.

sources.label: Australasian Menopause Society: Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause
Cancer Australia: Managing Menopausal Symptoms after Breast Cancer

subtopic_detail: Initial management of symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 56 year old woman who describes a dragging sensation and a feeling of something coming down that is worst by the end of the day. She has three children delivered vaginally, the youngest aged 22, and has not sought treatment for this before.

She has no urinary incontinence and no bowel symptoms. On examination the anterior vaginal wall descends to 1 cm above the hymen on straining with the cervix well supported. She works as a childcare educator and has completed her family.

data_table.Examination: Anterior compartment descent to 1 cm above the hymen on Valsalva, cervix well supported, no vault descent
data_table.Investigations: Post-void residual volume 30 mL; urinalysis shows no infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for anterior colporrhaphy with the aim of restoring anterior wall support
options.rationale: Surgery is considered after conservative measures fail, and offering it for early stage prolapse exposes her to recurrence and operative risk unnecessarily (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse).

options.text: Refer for supervised pelvic floor muscle training over at least sixteen weeks
options.rationale: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training improves prolapse symptoms and the objective stage in mild to moderate disease and is the recommended first line intervention (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse; Continence Foundation of Australia).

options.text: Fit a ring pessary at this visit and arrange a review appointment in six months
options.rationale: Pessaries are effective and appropriate for many women, but they are offered alongside or after physiotherapy rather than fitted before conservative therapy has been tried (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse).

options.text: Prescribe vaginal oestrogen cream as sole therapy and review in three months
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen improves tissue quality and is a useful adjunct, particularly before pessary use or surgery, but it does not correct descent on its own (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance defaecating proctography to define the compartments involved
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for complex or discordant presentations, and clinical staging is sufficient in straightforward anterior compartment prolapse (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic Organ Prolapse).

explanation.summary: Pelvic organ prolapse is staged clinically by the leading edge relative to the hymen, and treatment is driven by symptoms rather than by stage alone. Conservative management with supervised pelvic floor muscle training, weight management, constipation treatment and avoidance of repetitive heavy lifting is the starting point for mild to moderate symptomatic prolapse. Pessaries offer effective mechanical support for women who want to avoid surgery or who have not completed their family. Surgery is reserved for symptomatic prolapse that fails conservative care, with the choice of procedure guided by the compartment involved and by whether the uterus is preserved.
key_points: Stage is defined by the leading edge relative to the hymen; treatment is symptom driven
Supervised pelvic floor training is first line for mild to moderate symptomatic prolapse
Pessaries suit women avoiding surgery or with family plans not yet complete
Vaginal oestrogen is an adjunct that improves tissue quality, not a treatment for descent
Imaging is reserved for complex or discordant presentations
explanation.pearls: Supervised programs need at least sixteen weeks of training with a pelvic floor physiotherapist to show benefit, and unsupervised leaflet based exercises perform no better than no treatment in randomised comparisons.

subtopic_detail: Lactational mastitis not responding to milk removal
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar seeing a 29 year old woman three weeks postpartum who has had a painful red area in her left breast for 36 hours with fevers and shivers. The midwife reviewed her yesterday, corrected the attachment and advised frequent feeding from the affected side, which she has done.

She is still febrile and the red area has extended slightly. The breast is tender and firm over the upper outer quadrant with no discrete fluctuant lump and no nipple discharge. She has no penicillin allergy and her baby is feeding and gaining weight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98, BP 116/70, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Examination: Wedge shaped erythema over the left upper outer quadrant, firm and tender, no fluctuance, no axillary abscess
data_table.Investigations: Not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue effective milk removal alone and review again in a further 24 hours
options.rationale: Conservative measures are given 12 to 24 hours to work, and she has already had that period with spreading erythema and persistent fever (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Advise expressing and discarding milk from the affected breast during treatment
options.rationale: Discarding milk removes the infant from the affected side without benefit, and continued feeding is both safe and therapeutic because it maintains drainage (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association).

options.text: Arrange breast ultrasound before deciding whether antibiotic treatment is required
options.rationale: Ultrasound is indicated when an abscess is suspected from a fluctuant or persisting mass, and it should not delay antibiotics in a systemically unwell woman (Source: RANZCOG: Breastfeeding Problems).

options.text: Start oral dicloxacillin or flucloxacillin and continue feeding from both breasts
options.rationale: Failure of 24 hours of effective milk removal with systemic features indicates bacterial infection, and an antistaphylococcal penicillin is first line while breastfeeding continues (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Breastfeeding Association).

options.text: Start oral cefalexin and advise a temporary switch to formula feeding for five days
options.rationale: Cefalexin is an acceptable alternative agent, but stopping breastfeeding worsens stasis and is the single change most likely to lead to abscess formation (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association).

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis begins as inflammation from milk stasis and poor drainage, and only a proportion become bacterial. Initial management is effective milk removal with attention to attachment, along with analgesia and cold or warm compresses, reviewed at 12 to 24 hours. Antibiotics are added when there is no improvement after that period, when there are systemic features, or when a nipple fissure suggests entry of Staphylococcus aureus. Feeding continues throughout, because ongoing drainage is treatment; a persistent hard lump after adequate antibiotics suggests abscess and warrants ultrasound and aspiration.
key_points: Effective milk removal is the primary treatment and continues through antibiotic therapy
Antibiotics are added after 12 to 24 hours without improvement or if systemically unwell
Antistaphylococcal penicillins are first line; cefalexin or clindamycin cover allergy
Feeding from the affected breast is safe for the infant and reduces abscess risk
A persisting or fluctuant lump after treatment needs ultrasound and aspiration
explanation.pearls: An abscess in a lactating woman is managed by ultrasound guided needle aspiration rather than incision and drainage, which preserves the ability to keep feeding from that breast.

subtopic_detail: Intermediate risk result under the renewed screening program
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing results for a 33 year old woman who had her first cervical screening test two weeks ago after moving to Australia. She has no abnormal bleeding and no pain.

The laboratory reports oncogenic human papillomavirus detected, not types 16 or 18, with reflex liquid based cytology showing negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. She is not pregnant, uses a copper intrauterine device and is not immunosuppressed. She asks whether she needs a procedure.

data_table.Examination: Cervix appears macroscopically normal, no contact bleeding, intrauterine device threads visible
data_table.Investigations: Oncogenic human papillomavirus detected, not 16 or 18; reflex liquid based cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for colposcopy now because oncogenic human papillomavirus has been detected
options.rationale: Immediate colposcopy is for types 16 or 18, for any high grade cytology, or for a persisting intermediate risk result, none of which applies at this first test (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines).

options.text: Repeat the human papillomavirus test in twelve months and act on that result
options.rationale: Oncogenic types other than 16 and 18 with negative reflex cytology is the intermediate risk category, managed by a repeat test at twelve months because most infections clear spontaneously (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines; Cancer Council Australia).

options.text: Return to routine five yearly screening as the cytology showed no abnormality
options.rationale: Negative cytology does not return an intermediate risk woman to the five year interval, because persistent infection is the pathway to high grade disease (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines).

options.text: Repeat the screening test in six months and refer if the virus is still detected
options.rationale: A six month interval is too short to allow natural clearance and is not the program interval for this risk category (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines).

options.text: Offer human papillomavirus vaccination now and repeat the test after the course
options.rationale: Vaccination does not clear established infection or alter surveillance, though it may be discussed separately for protection against types not yet acquired (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

explanation.summary: The renewed program screens women aged 25 to 74 every five years with a primary human papillomavirus test and reflex cytology on the same sample. Results fall into three risk categories: higher risk with types 16 or 18 or high grade cytology, which goes to colposcopy; intermediate risk with other oncogenic types and negative or low grade cytology, which is repeated at twelve months; and lower risk, which returns to routine screening. Around 80 per cent of intermediate risk women clear the virus by the twelve month test and return to routine screening. Persistence at twelve months, or any high grade cytology at any point, triggers colposcopy.
key_points: Primary human papillomavirus testing every five years from age 25 to 74
Types 16 or 18 or high grade cytology means colposcopy
Other oncogenic types with negative cytology means a repeat test at twelve months
Most intermediate risk infections clear within twelve months
Self collected samples are available across the program and perform equivalently for oncogenic types
explanation.pearls: If the same non-16 or 18 oncogenic type is still detected at the twelve month repeat, colposcopy is indicated regardless of the cytology result, because it is persistence rather than the cytology that drives risk.

subtopic_detail: Ovulation induction in anovulatory polycystic ovary syndrome
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 28 year old woman who has been trying to conceive for sixteen months. She has four to five periods a year and has had facial hirsutism since her late teens.

Her body mass index is 32 kg/m2 and she has lost 4 kg with a dietitian over four months. Her partner's semen analysis is normal and a hysterosalpingogram shows both tubes patent with a normal uterine cavity. Thyroid function and prolactin are within normal limits and she has been taking folic acid for six months.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 32 kg/m2, Ferriman-Gallwey score 12, no acanthosis nigricans, no clitoromegaly
data_table.Investigations: Anti-Mullerian hormone elevated for age; mid-luteal progesterone 4 nmol/L on two cycles (ovulatory more than 20); HbA1c 38 mmol/mol (less than 42); thyroid function and prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment to achieve pregnancy?

options.text: Metformin as a single agent titrated to 1.5 g daily over four weeks
options.rationale: Metformin improves ovulation rates modestly and is an adjunct or alternative, but it is inferior to letrozole for live birth in this setting (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome).
source_refs: International Evidence-Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

options.text: Combined oral contraception for three cycles to regulate her menstrual pattern
options.rationale: Combined contraception regulates bleeding and treats hyperandrogenism but prevents conception, which is the stated goal (Source: RANZCOG: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome).

options.text: Letrozole for five days early in the cycle with monitoring of the response
options.rationale: Letrozole is the recommended first line ovulation induction agent in this condition, with higher ovulation and live birth rates than clomiphene, particularly at higher body mass index (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome; RANZCOG: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome).
source_refs: International Evidence-Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

options.text: Referral for in vitro fertilisation with a single embryo transfer policy
options.rationale: Assisted reproduction is reserved for failure of ovulation induction or another indication, and skipping to it exposes her to unnecessary cost and hyperstimulation risk (Source: RANZCOG: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome).

options.text: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling as a definitive treatment for her anovulatory cycles
options.rationale: Ovarian drilling is a second line option for clomiphene resistance and carries adhesion and reduced reserve risks that make it unsuitable as an opening move (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome).
source_refs: International Evidence-Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

explanation.summary: Polycystic ovary syndrome is the commonest cause of anovulatory infertility, diagnosed on two of three criteria: oligo-ovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovarian morphology, with anti-Mullerian hormone now accepted as an alternative to ultrasound morphology in adults. Before ovulation induction, tubal patency and semen analysis are confirmed so that a treatable co-factor is not missed. Letrozole is first line because it produces higher live birth rates than clomiphene without the antioestrogenic endometrial effect, and metformin is added for those with insulin resistance or clomiphene resistance. Weight loss of five to ten per cent improves ovulation independently and is pursued alongside rather than instead of drug therapy.
key_points: Diagnosis requires two of oligo-ovulation, hyperandrogenism and polycystic morphology or raised anti-Mullerian hormone
Confirm tubal patency and semen analysis before ovulation induction
Letrozole is first line and outperforms clomiphene, especially at higher body mass index
Metformin is adjunctive rather than a primary fertility agent
Five to ten per cent weight loss independently improves ovulation
explanation.pearls: Letrozole is given as 2.5 mg daily for five days from cycle day two to six, and the mid-luteal progesterone on that cycle confirms whether ovulation occurred before the dose is escalated.

sources.label: International Evidence-Based Guideline for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

subtopic_detail: Outpatient treatment of pelvic inflammatory disease
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 22 year old woman with five days of lower abdominal pain, deep pain with intercourse and an increase in vaginal discharge. Her last menstrual period was twelve days ago and a urine pregnancy test is negative.

She has had two new partners in the past three months and uses condoms inconsistently. On bimanual examination she has cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness with no palpable mass. She is tolerating oral fluids and has no allergies, and transvaginal ultrasound shows no tubo-ovarian collection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 114/70, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.6
data_table.Examination: Cervical motion tenderness, bilateral adnexal tenderness, mucopurulent cervical discharge, no mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative; endocervical nucleic acid amplification testing pending; white cells 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); transvaginal ultrasound shows no collection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to start now?

options.text: Oral azithromycin as a single dose with repeat testing for cure in four weeks
options.rationale: Single dose azithromycin treats uncomplicated cervical chlamydia but does not cover the polymicrobial and anaerobic component of upper tract infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Await the nucleic acid amplification results and treat according to the organism
options.rationale: Treatment is started on clinical grounds because delay increases tubal damage and infertility, and a substantial proportion of cases have no organism identified (Source: Australasian Sexual and Reproductive Health Alliance: STI Management Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Sexual and Reproductive Health Alliance: STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin with surgical review arranged
options.rationale: Inpatient parenteral therapy is for pregnancy, severe illness, failed oral treatment or a tubo-ovarian abscess, and the ultrasound excludes the last of these (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral doxycycline for fourteen days with metronidazole for the same duration
options.rationale: This pair covers chlamydia and anaerobes but omits gonococcal cover, which is required empirically given her risk profile (Source: Australasian Sexual and Reproductive Health Alliance: STI Management Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Sexual and Reproductive Health Alliance: STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Ceftriaxone intramuscularly with oral doxycycline and metronidazole for fourteen days
options.rationale: Australian outpatient therapy combines a single ceftriaxone dose for gonococcus with fourteen days of doxycycline for chlamydia and metronidazole for anaerobes, started before results return (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australasian Sexual and Reproductive Health Alliance: STI Management Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Sexual and Reproductive Health Alliance: STI Management Guidelines

explanation.summary: Pelvic inflammatory disease is a clinical diagnosis based on pelvic pain with cervical motion or adnexal tenderness in a sexually active woman, and the threshold to treat is deliberately low because each delayed episode adds to tubal infertility and ectopic pregnancy risk. Empirical therapy must cover gonococcus, chlamydia, anaerobes and Mycoplasma genitalium considerations, which is why three agents are used. Partner notification and treatment, testing for other sexually transmitted infections including human immunodeficiency virus and syphilis, and review at 48 to 72 hours all form part of management. Failure to improve at review prompts reassessment for abscess, an alternative diagnosis or non-adherence.
key_points: Diagnose clinically and treat empirically; do not wait for organism results
Outpatient therapy is ceftriaxone plus doxycycline and metronidazole for fourteen days
Admission is for pregnancy, severe illness, abscess or failed oral therapy
Partner notification and full sexually transmitted infection screening are part of treatment
Review at 48 to 72 hours; lack of improvement suggests abscess or an alternative diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Right upper quadrant pain with pelvic infection suggests perihepatitis, the Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, which does not change the antibiotic regimen but explains pain that otherwise prompts hepatobiliary imaging.

sources.label: Australasian Sexual and Reproductive Health Alliance: STI Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Folate dosing and antiseizure medicine review
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar seeing a 27 year old woman who plans to conceive in the next six months. She has generalised epilepsy that has been seizure free for three years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, having previously failed lamotrigine because of a rash.

She takes no other medicines, does not smoke and has a body mass index of 23 kg/m2. She has no personal or family history of neural tube defect and her diet includes fortified breads and cereals. She asks what she should do before stopping contraception.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Arrange urgent neurology review to change medicine and start high dose folate
options.rationale: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk of the antiseizure medicines and warrants a planned switch before conception, alongside 5 mg folic acid daily rather than the standard dose (Source: RANZCOG: Pre-pregnancy Counselling; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose and start folic acid 500 micrograms daily
options.rationale: The standard dose applies to women without risk factors, and continuing valproate unchanged accepts a dose dependent risk that planning can reduce (Source: RANZCOG: Pre-pregnancy Counselling).

options.text: Stop valproate immediately and start folic acid 5 mg daily from next month
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal of an effective antiseizure medicine risks status epilepticus, which is more dangerous to mother and foetus than a supervised transition (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Continue valproate and arrange detailed morphology scanning at nineteen weeks
options.rationale: Morphology scanning detects structural defects but cannot detect the neurodevelopmental harm that dominates valproate risk, and detection is not prevention (Source: RANZCOG: Pre-pregnancy Counselling).

options.text: Rechallenge with lamotrigine now and start folic acid 500 micrograms daily
options.rationale: Rechallenge after a drug rash needs specialist supervision and slow titration, and the folate dose here is the one for women without risk factors (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Preconception care is where most modifiable pregnancy risk is addressed, because organogenesis is largely complete before many women present for antenatal care. Folic acid 400 to 500 micrograms daily from at least one month before conception until twelve weeks is standard, with 5 mg daily for women with a previous affected pregnancy, diabetes, obesity, malabsorption or those taking antiseizure medicines. Valproate exposure in utero carries roughly a ten per cent risk of major malformation and a substantially higher risk of impaired neurodevelopment, both dose dependent, so a planned switch under neurology supervision is made before conception rather than after a positive test. Seizure control itself protects the pregnancy, so medicines are never stopped abruptly.
key_points: Standard folic acid is 400 to 500 micrograms daily from one month before conception to twelve weeks
High dose 5 mg is used with antiseizure medicines, diabetes, obesity, malabsorption or a previous affected pregnancy
Valproate has the highest malformation and neurodevelopmental risk of the antiseizure medicines
Medicine changes happen before conception and under specialist supervision
Never stop an effective antiseizure medicine abruptly
explanation.pearls: Valproate in utero is associated with about a 30 to 40 per cent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment and an eight to nine point mean reduction in childhood IQ, which is why the decision is made before conception, not at the first antenatal visit.

subtopic_detail: Human chorionic gonadotrophin surveillance after molar evacuation
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31 year old woman seven weeks after suction evacuation of a histologically confirmed complete hydatidiform mole. She has had no further bleeding and no abdominal pain and is using combined oral contraception.

Her serum human chorionic gonadotrophin has been measured weekly. The last four values are 3120, 2980, 3050 and 2990 IU/L. Examination shows no vaginal lesion and her chest is clear. A repeat pelvic ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a slightly heterogeneous myometrial echo pattern.

data_table.Examination: Uterus not palpable abdominally, no vaginal lesion, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Serial weekly human chorionic gonadotrophin 3120, 2980, 3050 and 2990 IU/L; haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-155); thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue weekly surveillance and repeat the ultrasound in a further four weeks
options.rationale: Continued observation is appropriate while values fall, but a plateau across four consecutive weekly samples has already met the threshold for a new diagnosis (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease).

options.text: Arrange repeat suction evacuation of the uterine cavity under ultrasound guidance
options.rationale: A second evacuation is considered only for significant retained tissue on imaging, and it rarely avoids chemotherapy once a plateau is established (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease).

options.text: Refer to a gestational trophoblastic disease centre for staging and treatment
options.rationale: Four consecutive plateaued weekly values over three weeks defines post-molar gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is staged and treated at a specialist centre rather than managed locally (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease; Cancer Council Australia).

options.text: Cease the combined oral contraception as it is suppressing the fall in the marker
options.rationale: Hormonal contraception is recommended during surveillance and does not delay the fall in the marker, which was the historical concern (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease).

options.text: Arrange total abdominal hysterectomy as definitive management of the plateau
options.rationale: Hysterectomy sits on a different treatment axis and is reserved for older women who have completed childbearing or for uncontrolled bleeding, since chemotherapy is highly curative and preserves fertility (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

explanation.summary: After evacuation of a hydatidiform mole, human chorionic gonadotrophin is followed serially because persistent trophoblastic tissue can develop into gestational trophoblastic neoplasia in around 15 per cent of complete moles and 1 to 5 per cent of partial moles. Neoplasia is diagnosed by a plateau across four values over three weeks, a rise of ten per cent or more across three values over two weeks, persistence beyond six months, or histological choriocarcinoma. Staging then uses the anatomical stage with the prognostic score to separate low risk disease, treated with single agent methotrexate or dactinomycin, from high risk disease needing multi-agent chemotherapy. Cure rates approach 100 per cent in low risk disease with fertility usually preserved.
key_points: Around 15 per cent of complete moles progress to neoplasia and need chemotherapy
A plateau over four values across three weeks defines neoplasia
A rise of ten per cent or more across three values over two weeks is the alternative criterion
Hormonal contraception is used during surveillance and does not interfere with the marker
Low risk disease is cured with single agent chemotherapy with fertility usually preserved
explanation.pearls: Pregnancy is avoided until the marker has been normal for at least six months, because a new pregnancy makes the surveillance marker uninterpretable and masks recurrence.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease

subtopic_detail: Persisting vulval plaque despite potent topical corticosteroid
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 67 year old woman with biopsy proven vulval lichen sclerosus diagnosed four years ago. She has used clobetasol propionate ointment as directed and her itch has settled everywhere except one area.

On the left labium majus there is a 12 mm firm white thickened plaque that has been present for five months and has not changed with treatment. The surrounding skin shows the pale atrophic change and architectural loss typical of her condition, without fissuring or ulceration. Her adherence has been confirmed by tube counts at each review and she has no vaginal discharge.

data_table.Examination: 12 mm firm hyperkeratotic plaque on the left labium majus, surrounding pallor and loss of architecture, no ulcer, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Vulval swab shows no candida or bacterial pathogen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a punch biopsy of the thickened plaque and continue her current ointment
options.rationale: A localised area that fails to respond to adequate potent corticosteroid must be biopsied to exclude differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia or invasive squamous carcinoma (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Skin Disorders; Australasian College of Dermatologists).

options.text: Escalate to a more potent corticosteroid under occlusion and review in three months
options.rationale: Clobetasol is already the most potent class available, and adding occlusion delays diagnosis of a lesion that has been static for five months (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Skin Disorders).

options.text: Change to topical tacrolimus ointment twice daily and reassess in three months
options.rationale: Calcineurin inhibitors are second line for corticosteroid intolerance, and they carry a theoretical malignancy concern that makes them a poor choice for undiagnosed thickened skin (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to stage the vulval abnormality
options.rationale: Imaging is a staging tool once malignancy is confirmed histologically, and it cannot characterise a 12 mm cutaneous plaque (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

options.text: Prescribe a course of oral prednisolone and review the plaque again in six weeks
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroid has no established role in this condition and would suppress an inflammatory appearance without excluding neoplasia (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Skin Disorders).

explanation.summary: Vulval lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis treated with ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, initially daily and then reduced to maintenance, with long term maintenance shown to reduce both symptoms and progression. Lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma is around 2 to 5 per cent, and the pathway is usually through differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, which does not have the papillomavirus association of the usual type. Any area that is fixed, ulcerated, eroded or hyperkeratotic, or that fails to respond to adequate treatment, is biopsied rather than treated more intensively. Long term annual review is recommended, with earlier review for any new lesion.
key_points: Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line, with long term maintenance reducing cancer risk
Lifetime squamous cell carcinoma risk is about 2 to 5 per cent
Differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia is the precursor and is not papillomavirus related
Any non-responding, ulcerated or hyperkeratotic area requires biopsy
Adherence is checked before treatment is declared to have failed
explanation.pearls: Differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia progresses to invasive carcinoma faster than the usual papillomavirus related type, often within one to two years, which is why a static plaque on treated lichen sclerosus is biopsied rather than watched.

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a single positive antiphospholipid result
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman who has had three first trimester losses, the most recent six weeks ago. She has one healthy child born at term and no thrombotic history.

Bloods taken at the time of the most recent loss show a positive lupus anticoagulant and a negative anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I. Parental karyotypes are normal, pelvic ultrasound shows a normal uterine cavity, and thyroid function and HbA1c are within normal limits. She is not pregnant now and is asking whether she should start treatment before trying again.

data_table.Examination: No livedo, no leg swelling, no synovitis
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant positive at the time of loss; anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I negative; thyroid function and HbA1c within normal limits; pelvic ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start aspirin and prophylactic enoxaparin now and continue through the next pregnancy
options.rationale: Combined therapy is the correct treatment once the syndrome is confirmed, but committing to injections on a single unconfirmed result over-treats a result that often does not persist (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent Miscarriage).

options.text: Start low dose aspirin alone and repeat the full antibody panel during pregnancy
options.rationale: Aspirin alone is inferior to combined therapy in confirmed disease, and testing during pregnancy is unreliable because pregnancy and anticoagulants both distort the assays (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent Miscarriage).

options.text: Reassure her that three first trimester losses need no further testing or treatment
options.rationale: Three consecutive losses is the threshold for investigation in Australian practice, and she has a result that requires interpretation rather than dismissal (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent Miscarriage).

options.text: Start prednisolone through the first trimester and repeat the panel after delivery
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not improve live birth rates in this setting and add gestational diabetes and preterm birth risk (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Antiphospholipid Syndrome).

options.text: Repeat the antibody testing at least twelve weeks apart before labelling and treating
options.rationale: Classification requires the same antibody positive on two occasions at least twelve weeks apart, and a single result taken at the time of a pregnancy loss is frequently transient (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent Miscarriage; BMJ Best Practice: Antiphospholipid Syndrome).

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage is investigated after three consecutive first trimester losses, or earlier when the woman is older or has other risk factors, with testing directed at antiphospholipid antibodies, uterine anatomy, thyroid function, glycaemic control and parental karyotype where the history suggests it. Antiphospholipid syndrome is the one clearly treatable cause, but its classification deliberately requires persistence of the same antibody on two occasions at least twelve weeks apart, since transient positivity follows infection, pregnancy loss and some drugs. Confirmed obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome is treated with low dose aspirin plus prophylactic low molecular weight heparin from the confirmation of pregnancy, which raises live birth rates substantially. Most couples with unexplained recurrent loss still achieve a live birth with supportive care alone.
key_points: Investigate after three consecutive first trimester losses in Australian practice
Antiphospholipid classification needs the same antibody positive twice, at least twelve weeks apart
Transient positivity follows infection, pregnancy loss and some drugs
Confirmed obstetric disease is treated with aspirin plus prophylactic low molecular weight heparin
Corticosteroids have no role and add pregnancy complications
explanation.pearls: Lupus anticoagulant testing cannot be interpreted while a woman is on an anticoagulant or during acute illness, so the confirmatory sample is timed for when she is well and untreated.

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding during tamoxifen therapy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 61 year old woman with two episodes of light vaginal bleeding in the past month. She is four years into tamoxifen for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer and her last menstrual period was at age 51.

Transvaginal ultrasound reports an endometrial thickness of 9 mm with a cystic subendometrial appearance and no focal lesion identified. She takes no anticoagulant, the vaginal epithelium appears healthy, and her cervical screening is up to date and negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus.

data_table.Examination: Vulva and vagina healthy, cervix normal, uterus normal size, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Endometrial thickness 9 mm with cystic subendometrial change on transvaginal ultrasound; haemoglobin 131 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in three months and investigate if thickness increases
options.rationale: Surveillance imaging cannot exclude carcinoma in a woman who has already bled, and the tamoxifen related appearance will not resolve (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopy with directed endometrial biopsy under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Tamoxifen produces subendometrial cystic change that inflates the measured thickness and hides focal lesions, so the ultrasound threshold is unreliable and direct visualisation with biopsy is required (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding; Cancer Council Australia).

options.text: Reassure her that the thickness is below the threshold requiring further assessment
options.rationale: The 4 mm threshold applies to women not taking tamoxifen, and applying it here is the specific misstep this presentation tests (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding).

options.text: Cease tamoxifen and reassess the endometrium with imaging after three months
options.rationale: Stopping adjuvant endocrine therapy is an oncology decision with survival implications and does not answer the diagnostic question in front of her (Source: Cancer Australia).

options.text: Arrange pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to characterise the endometrial appearance
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is a staging tool after tissue diagnosis and cannot distinguish benign tamoxifen change from carcinoma (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding carries roughly a ten per cent risk of endometrial carcinoma and always requires assessment. In women not taking tamoxifen, an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less on transvaginal ultrasound has a high negative predictive value and can avoid biopsy, while thicker endometrium proceeds to sampling. Tamoxifen produces subepithelial stromal change with cystic spaces that artificially increases the measured thickness and obscures polyps and focal lesions, so the sonographic threshold does not apply and hysteroscopic assessment with directed biopsy is preferred. Tamoxifen roughly doubles to triples endometrial cancer risk in postmenopausal women, but asymptomatic surveillance is not recommended because it generates false positives without improving outcomes.
key_points: Postmenopausal bleeding carries about a ten per cent risk of endometrial carcinoma
The 4 mm ultrasound threshold applies only to women not taking tamoxifen
Tamoxifen causes cystic subendometrial change that inflates thickness and hides focal lesions
Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is preferred over blind sampling in these women
Asymptomatic endometrial surveillance during tamoxifen is not recommended
explanation.pearls: Blind pipelle sampling misses about half of focal endometrial lesions in tamoxifen users, which is the specific reason hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is chosen over an office sample in this group.

subtopic_detail: Severity assessment after oocyte retrieval
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 30 year old woman six days after oocyte retrieval in a fresh in vitro fertilisation cycle. She has abdominal distension, nausea and breathlessness when lying flat, and her weight is 4 kg above her pre-cycle baseline.

She passed only 300 mL of urine in the last 24 hours despite drinking. Ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries with moderate ascites and no adnexal torsion. Embryo transfer has not yet occurred and all embryos have been frozen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 98/60, RR 22, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Tense distended abdomen, shifting dullness, calves soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.49 (0.35-0.45); white cells 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); creatinine 104 micromol/L (45-90); sodium 130 mmol/L (135-145); albumin 27 g/L (35-50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Manage at home with oral fluids, daily weights and review in the clinic in 48 hours
options.rationale: Outpatient management suits mild to moderate disease with normal haematocrit and urine output, neither of which applies with haemoconcentration and oliguria (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome).

options.text: Admit for intravenous fluids with frusemide added to improve her urine output
options.rationale: Diuretics worsen intravascular depletion and thrombotic risk in a condition driven by third space fluid shift, and are reserved for oliguria persisting after volume repletion (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome).

options.text: Admit for observation with oral fluids alone and repeat the bloods in the morning
options.rationale: Admission is right but withholding intravenous replacement and thromboprophylaxis leaves the two processes that cause harm untreated (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome).

options.text: Admit for intravenous fluid replacement with thromboprophylaxis and paracentesis if needed
options.rationale: Haemoconcentration with oliguria, tense ascites and hypoalbuminaemia is severe disease, managed with volume replacement, low molecular weight heparin and drainage of ascites for symptoms or oliguria (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome; Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Arrange laparoscopy to drain the ascites and assess the ovaries for torsion
options.rationale: Surgery is avoided because enlarged ovaries bleed readily, and ultrasound has already shown no torsion, so drainage is done percutaneously (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome).

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome is an iatrogenic condition caused by vascular endothelial growth factor driven capillary leak after gonadotrophin stimulation, with human chorionic gonadotrophin as the trigger for the cascade. Early onset disease appears within nine days of the trigger injection, while late onset disease after that point reflects endogenous hormone from an implanting pregnancy and tends to be more severe and prolonged. Severity is graded on symptoms plus haematocrit, white cell count, albumin, renal function and the presence of ascites or effusion, and severe disease is admitted for volume replacement, thromboprophylaxis and consideration of paracentesis. Prevention through antagonist protocols, agonist triggers and freeze all strategies has reduced severe cases substantially.
key_points: Vascular endothelial growth factor driven capillary leak underlies the syndrome
Haematocrit, white cell count, albumin and urine output grade severity
Severe disease needs admission, intravenous replacement and low molecular weight heparin
Diuretics are avoided until intravascular volume is restored
Freeze all embryo strategies and agonist triggers prevent late onset severe disease
explanation.pearls: Thromboprophylaxis in severe hyperstimulation continues for several weeks after resolution, and thrombosis characteristically occurs in the upper limb and neck veins rather than the legs, so unusual sites do not exclude the diagnosis.

sources.label: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand
BMJ Best Practice: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome

subtopic_detail: Assessment before surgery for mixed urinary incontinence
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 54 year old woman with four years of urinary leakage. She leaks with coughing and also has sudden urgency with leakage on the way to the toilet, and she cannot say which is more troublesome.

She has completed six months of supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy and a three month trial of an antimuscarinic with partial benefit only. Her bladder diary shows nine voids daily with two urgency episodes and no nocturia. Post-void residual volume is 40 mL, urinalysis shows no infection and no haematuria, and she is now asking about surgery.

data_table.Examination: Stress leak demonstrated on cough with a full bladder, no prolapse beyond the hymen, good pelvic floor contraction
data_table.Investigations: Post-void residual 40 mL; urinalysis negative for nitrites, leucocytes and blood; bladder diary shows nine voids daily and two urgency episodes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to mid-urethral sling surgery on the basis of the demonstrated stress leak
options.rationale: Operating without characterising the urgency component risks worsening storage symptoms after surgery and leaves the woman unable to give properly informed consent (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women).

options.text: Arrange urodynamic studies to define the relative contribution of each component
options.rationale: Urodynamics is indicated before continence surgery when symptoms are mixed or discordant with examination, because detrusor overactivity changes both the operative decision and the counselling about outcome (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women; Continence Foundation of Australia).

options.text: Start a second antimuscarinic agent and continue the physiotherapy program
options.rationale: Sequential antimuscarinics have diminishing returns and would repeat a trial that has already given partial benefit over three months (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology).

options.text: Arrange intravesical botulinum toxin injection for her urgency related symptoms
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin is third line for refractory overactive bladder and requires the ability to self-catheterise, so it is not chosen before the components are defined (Source: Continence Foundation of Australia).

options.text: Prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen and review her symptoms again in six months
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen helps urgency associated with atrophy and is a useful adjunct, but it does not address a demonstrated stress component (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

explanation.summary: Urinary incontinence is characterised first by history, bladder diary, examination with a cough stress test, urinalysis and post-void residual, and most women are managed conservatively with pelvic floor training, weight loss, caffeine reduction and bladder training. Antimuscarinics or a beta-3 agonist are added for urgency predominant symptoms, with attention to anticholinergic burden in older women. Urodynamics is not needed for straightforward stress incontinence proceeding to surgery, but is recommended when symptoms are mixed, when previous surgery has failed, when voiding dysfunction is suspected or when the findings do not match the history. Mid-urethral sling surgery remains effective for stress incontinence, and Australian practice requires documented informed consent covering mesh specific risks.
key_points: Bladder diary, cough stress test, urinalysis and post-void residual form the initial assessment
Conservative therapy precedes both drugs and surgery
Urodynamics is indicated for mixed or discordant symptoms before continence surgery
Detrusor overactivity predicts persisting urgency after sling surgery and alters counselling
Mesh procedures require documented consent covering device specific risks
explanation.pearls: Urgency persists after a mid-urethral sling in roughly a third of women with mixed incontinence and can worsen, which is the specific outcome that urodynamic characterisation lets you quantify before consent.

subtopic_detail: Suspected deep disease with urinary tract involvement
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 34 year old woman with eight years of increasingly severe period pain and deep pain with intercourse. For the past year she has noticed blood in her urine for two days at the start of each period and has had two courses of antibiotics for presumed infection.

Urine cultures taken during those episodes were negative. She has been on a continuous combined oral contraceptive for six months with partial benefit and has no bowel symptoms. Transvaginal ultrasound performed at a general radiology practice was reported as normal, and renal function is preserved.

data_table.Examination: Tenderness and nodularity in the posterior fornix, fixed retroverted uterus, no adnexal mass palpable
data_table.Investigations: Two urine cultures negative during symptomatic episodes; creatinine 72 micromol/L (45-90); transvaginal ultrasound reported normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat urine culture during the next episode and treat with a longer antibiotic course
options.rationale: Two negative cultures during symptoms already exclude infection, and repeating them delays assessment of a cyclical pattern that infection does not explain (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis).

options.text: Proceed directly to diagnostic laparoscopy without further imaging beforehand
options.rationale: Laparoscopy remains important, but operating without mapping deep and urinary tract disease risks an incomplete procedure without the urological input it may require (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis).

options.text: Add a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for three months and reassess symptoms
options.rationale: Medical suppression may relieve pain but does not detect silent ureteric obstruction, which can destroy renal function without symptoms (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis).

options.text: Arrange specialist pelvic imaging assessing the ureters, bladder and posterior compartment
options.rationale: Cyclical haematuria with posterior fornix nodularity indicates deep disease with urinary tract involvement, and dedicated endometriosis protocol imaging maps the ureters and bladder before any surgical planning (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis; Australian Living Evidence Guideline: Endometriosis).

options.text: Arrange cystoscopy alone to visualise and biopsy any bladder lesions present
options.rationale: Cystoscopy sees bladder mucosal disease but misses ureteric involvement and the posterior compartment, so it is an adjunct rather than the mapping investigation (Source: Australian Living Evidence Guideline: Endometriosis).

explanation.summary: Endometriosis is diagnosed clinically and imaging is used to identify deep disease, not to exclude the condition, since a normal scan never rules it out. Standard transvaginal ultrasound performed without an endometriosis protocol misses most deep infiltrating disease, so specialist imaging or a dedicated protocol scan is arranged when examination or symptoms suggest it. Urinary tract involvement occurs in around 1 to 5 per cent of cases and is important because ureteric disease can cause silent obstruction and irreversible renal loss with no urinary symptoms at all. Management of deep disease is planned in a multidisciplinary setting with colorectal and urological input where indicated, alongside hormonal suppression and pain management.
key_points: A normal ultrasound does not exclude endometriosis
Standard ultrasound misses most deep infiltrating disease without a dedicated protocol
Cyclical haematuria with negative cultures suggests urinary tract involvement
Ureteric disease can obstruct silently and cause irreversible renal loss
Deep disease surgery is planned with urological and colorectal input
explanation.pearls: Around a third of women with ureteric endometriosis have no urinary symptoms at all, so a renal tract assessment is arranged whenever deep posterior compartment disease is suspected, not only when haematuria is present.

subtopic_detail: Chronic insomnia first line treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 44 year old accountant who has had trouble getting to sleep and staying asleep on five nights a week for nine months. She lies awake for up to two hours and then watches the clock, and she is irritable and unproductive at work.

She drinks one coffee before midday and uses no alcohol or other substances. She has no depressive or anxiety disorder on structured assessment, her thyroid function is within normal limits, and her partner has never heard her snore or stop breathing. A sleep diary shows eight and a half hours in bed for about five and a half hours of sleep, and she has already removed her phone from the bedroom without benefit.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, no goitre, mental state examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, full blood count and ferritin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia including sleep restriction
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line for chronic insomnia disorder, and the excessive time in bed with poor sleep efficiency is precisely what its sleep restriction component targets (Source: RACGP: Management of Chronic Insomnia; Sleep Health Foundation Australia).

options.text: Prescribe temazepam at night for four weeks and review her sleep diary after that
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are for short term situational insomnia only, and starting one in a nine month problem sets up tolerance and rebound insomnia on withdrawal (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Prescribe low dose amitriptyline at night and review her symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antidepressants are prescribed off label for sleep but have anticholinergic effects and no evidence base as first line in primary insomnia (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Prescribe melatonin modified release nightly and review her symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Modified release melatonin is approved for people aged 55 and over and has modest effects on sleep onset, so it does not displace structured therapy here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Provide written sleep hygiene advice alone and review her sleep diary in six weeks
options.rationale: Sleep hygiene as a standalone intervention performs poorly in trials and is the weakest component of the therapy package rather than a substitute for it (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia).

explanation.summary: Chronic insomnia disorder requires difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep at least three nights a week for at least three months, with daytime consequences, in the presence of adequate opportunity to sleep. Assessment excludes contributors such as obstructive sleep apnoea, restless legs, shift work, substances, pain and untreated mood or anxiety disorder. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia combines stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive restructuring and relaxation, and it outperforms hypnotics at follow up because its gains persist after treatment ends. Australian access has broadened through digital programs and psychologists trained in the model, which matters where face to face therapy is limited.
key_points: Diagnosis requires three nights weekly for three months with daytime impairment
Exclude sleep apnoea, restless legs, substances and untreated mood or anxiety disorder
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and its gains persist after treatment
Sleep restriction targets low sleep efficiency and is the most active ingredient
Hypnotics are short term adjuncts, not maintenance therapy
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction sets time in bed to the average total sleep time from the diary, never below five hours, then extends it by fifteen minutes each week once sleep efficiency exceeds 85 per cent.

subtopic_detail: Gambling disorder identification and initial management
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 38 year old man referred after presenting to his general practitioner with insomnia and low mood. On questioning he describes betting on sport through a phone application most evenings, increasing his stakes over two years to chase losses.

He has hidden a personal loan from his partner and has twice tried to stop for a month without success. He drinks two standard drinks a week and uses no other substances. He denies current suicidal intent but says he has thought that his family would be better off without him, and his mood improves on days when he does not bet.

data_table.Examination: Mildly anxious, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence an antidepressant for the depressive symptoms and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants do not treat the disorder itself and his mood tracks his betting, so treating mood alone leaves the driver of the presentation untouched (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence naltrexone and arrange psychiatric review of his mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Opioid antagonists show benefit in some trials but are an adjunct after psychological therapy has been organised, not the opening intervention (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Refer for structured psychological therapy with safety assessment and self-exclusion advice
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy is the best evidenced treatment, and it is paired with a suicide risk assessment and practical harm reduction such as national self-exclusion registration and financial safeguards (Source: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register

options.text: Advise him to disclose the debt to his partner and review his progress in six weeks
options.rationale: Disclosure is often part of recovery but is his decision to time, and advice alone provides no treatment for a disorder with a high relapse rate (Source: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register).
source_refs: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register

options.text: Admit to an inpatient unit for supervised withdrawal from gambling behaviours
options.rationale: There is no physiological withdrawal syndrome requiring admission, and inpatient care is reserved for acute suicide risk or severe comorbidity (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is classified with the substance related and addictive disorders because of shared features of tolerance, withdrawal-like irritability, loss of control and chasing losses. It is strongly associated with depression, anxiety, alcohol use disorder and suicide, with suicide risk several times that of the general population, so risk assessment is part of every consultation. Cognitive behavioural therapy has the strongest evidence, delivered face to face, by telephone or online, alongside financial counselling and practical barriers such as the national self-exclusion register and bank gambling blocks. Comorbid depression is treated in its own right when it does not remit as gambling reduces.
key_points: Classified with addictive disorders and shares tolerance and loss of control features
Suicide risk is markedly elevated and is assessed at every contact
Cognitive behavioural therapy is the best evidenced treatment
Self-exclusion registration, bank blocks and financial counselling are practical adjuncts
Treat comorbid depression separately if it persists as gambling reduces
explanation.pearls: The national self-exclusion register blocks a person from all licensed Australian online and telephone wagering operators for a chosen period of at least three months, and registration is a concrete first session task rather than general advice.

sources.label: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register

subtopic_detail: Initial approach to an adult seeking gender affirming care
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 24 year old trans woman referred by her general practitioner for an opinion before starting feminising hormone therapy. She has identified as female since her mid teens, has socially transitioned for two years and uses her chosen name at work.

She describes persistent low mood and social anxiety that she attributes to family rejection and to workplace misgendering, with no self-harm and no psychotic symptoms. She has capacity, is not intoxicated and has read reputable material about the effects and limits of hormone therapy. Her general practitioner has asked whether her mood symptoms mean treatment should be deferred.

data_table.Examination: Mood mildly low with reactive affect, no thought disorder, no suicidal intent, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function, renal function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Defer hormone therapy until her depressive and anxiety symptoms have fully remitted
options.rationale: Requiring full remission before affirming care sets a threshold not applied to other treatments and delays an intervention that itself improves mood (Source: AusPATH Standards of Care; RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity

options.text: Request a two year documented real life experience before supporting hormone therapy
options.rationale: Mandatory real life experience requirements have been removed from contemporary standards as a barrier without evidence of benefit (Source: AusPATH Standards of Care).

options.text: Commence a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review the gender question in six months
options.rationale: Medicating distress that arises largely from rejection and misgendering, while postponing the affirming intervention, treats the symptom and not the situation (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity

options.text: Advise that psychiatric assessment is mandatory before any hormone can be prescribed
options.rationale: Australian standards support an informed consent model delivered by experienced prescribers, with mental health input available rather than compulsory (Source: AusPATH Standards of Care).

options.text: Support hormone therapy now and treat her mood symptoms alongside it
options.rationale: Coexisting mood or anxiety symptoms are not a barrier to affirming care when capacity is intact, and gender affirming hormone therapy is associated with improved psychological outcomes while the mood symptoms are treated concurrently (Source: AusPATH Standards of Care; RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity

explanation.summary: Contemporary Australian standards for adult gender affirming care use an informed consent model in which capacity, understanding of the effects and limits of treatment, and management of relevant medical risks are what matter, rather than psychiatric gatekeeping. Mental health problems are common in trans and gender diverse populations and largely reflect minority stress, family rejection and discrimination, so they are treated alongside affirming care rather than as a precondition for it. Psychiatric input is valuable where diagnostic uncertainty, significant mental illness affecting capacity, or complex comorbidity exists. Cohort data consistently show improvement in depression, anxiety and quality of life after commencing affirming hormone therapy.
key_points: Adult care follows an informed consent model, not compulsory psychiatric approval
Real life experience requirements have been removed from current standards
Coexisting mood and anxiety symptoms are treated alongside affirming care
Minority stress explains much of the psychological distress in this population
Psychiatric input is for capacity concerns, diagnostic uncertainty or complex comorbidity
explanation.pearls: Feminising hormone therapy produces breast development and body fat redistribution over one to two years but does not change voice pitch, which is why speech pathology referral is discussed at the same visit rather than after treatment disappoints.
